title: Adelaide laneway named in honour of hip hop pioneers Hilltop Hoods
text:
Pioneering Australian hip hop group Hilltop Hoods rapped about "Goin' down a hard road" in 2006.

Now, the Adelaide trio are being honoured with a laneway in their hometown.

Clubhouse Lane, running off Hindley Street in Adelaide's CBD, was renamed Hilltop Hoods Lane at a ceremony today.

Two large-scale murals featuring the group and their associated iconography, created by Adelaide artist Vans the Omega, run down both sides of the laneway.

The Hoods, who still call Adelaide home, say it's an "incredible honour" to have their own laneway in the heart of the city they know and love.

"We have great memories of gigging in that part of town," Pressure told Double J's Dylan Lewis.

" When we were paying our dues and coming up there was heaps of old bars and clubs that we used to play. Some of them are still there, some are not. "

Hilltop Hoods members Pressure, Suffa and DJ Debris pose with the street sign from their titular laneway. (Supplied: Ashlee Jones)

Paying tribute to one of Australia's most successful and enduring musical acts, Hilltop Hoods Lane is the sixth addition to City of Adelaide's City of Music Laneway trail.

The growing collection includes landmarks recognising South Australian music legends Cold Chisel, Sia, Paul Kelly, No Fixed Address, and The Angels.

Hilltop Hoods even have some suggestions for the next honorary music landmark.

"I reckon Funkoars need a lane! Surely Guy Sebastian should have one," they told Lewis. "Guy Lane? Does have a ring to it."

Hilltop Hoods' The Calling helped legitimise hip hop in Australia The Adelaide trio's third album encompasses so much more than 'The Nosebleed Section'.

Lord Mayor Jane Lomax-Smith said Hilltop Hoods's enduring impact on Australian music and culture made them a worthy addition to Adelaide's City of Music Laneways.

"Once considered the Australian music industry's underdogs, the Hoods have harnessed their talent and determination to not only top the charts but build a multi-generational fan base in their mosh pits," Dr Lomax-Smith said.

" Despite their global success, they have never forgotten their Adelaide roots. That's why it's fabulous to permanently recognise their achievements on the streets. "

Hilltop Hoods have more than 1 million album sales and 2 billion streams to their name. (Supplied: Lauren Connelly)

Starting as teenagers in 1994 around the hills of Blackwood, Hilltop Hoods elevated Australian hip hop from the underground and into the mainstream. And to resounding success.

The trio — Suffa (Matthew Lambert), Pressure (Dan Smith) and DJ Debris (Barry Francis) — have released a record-making seven ARIA number one albums, won 10 ARIA Awards, six APRA Awards, and sold out multiple national arena tours.

They have made triple j's annual Hottest 100 on a record 27 occasions, the most entries of any music group.

Their 2003 breakout single The Nosebleed Section came second place to INXS's poll-topping Never Tear Us Apart in last year's Hottest 100 of Australian Songs, in which they charted twice more (Cosby Sweater at #64 and 1955 at #73).

Hilltop Hoods remember Melanie, the late folk singer sampled on 'The Nosebleed Section' MC Suffa reflects on meeting the artist who powered the Hoods' breakout 2003 anthem.

"Few music acts are as deeply woven into the cultural fabric of South Australia as Hilltop Hoods," said Vans the Omega, wanting his artwork to honour their connection to devoted fans and the wider public alike.

"This work aims to be both uplifting and historic, offering a place to reflect on our own lives and the journey we have shared alongside music that has shaped generations of fans of all ages.

"Like the Hoods, these walls stand as a lasting testament to what can be achieved through hard work and determination in our beautiful, humble city of Adelaide."

The first Australian hip hop group to have a laneway named in their honour, Hilltop Hoods join a growing list of musical landmarks around the country. That includes lanes named for AC/DC and Chrissy Amphlett in Melbourne, and The Go Between Bridge in Brisbane.

title: Adelaide University to offer staff early retirements as financial woes grow
text:
Adelaide University says it may consider a round of voluntary redundancies and will offer staff early retirement packages, as it grapples with a worsening revenue shortfall from a downturn in international students.

The new merger university told staff on Thursday that it was opening expressions of interest for a "Voluntary Early Retirement Scheme (VERS)", available to employees over the age of 55 with five or more years of continuous service.

The university emphasised that the scheme was not a voluntary redundancy process, but one "may be considered in future" if it aligned with "broader workforce planning and institutional financial considerations".

The university said some roles vacated through the retirement scheme may be filled again, but "not every position will be replaced".

$500m Adelaide University merger squeezed by international student cuts The new Adelaide University is not on track to meet its international student targets, with the federal government's migration clampdown squeezing the business case for the newly merged institution.

"It is important to note that participation in the VERS is entirely voluntary," Adelaide University's head of people and culture, Joanne Fox, said in an all-staff email on Thursday afternoon.

" No one is expected or required to express interest, apply or retire. "

Ms Fox said the university had to "respond carefully to a changing operating environment", which included "sector-wide financial pressures arising from the international student recruitment outlook".

The university has previously said that its international student enrolments are 40 per cent below target, creating a projected revenue shortfall of around $90 million.

It has laid the blame squarely at the feet of the federal government's policy changes to bring down international student numbers, although its competitor, Flinders University, has had a 15 per cent increase in international onshore enrolments this year.

Professor Nicola Phillips says Adelaide University is managing cost carefully for the foreseeable future. (ABC News: Daniel Taylor)

In a pre-recorded video message to staff last week, Adelaide University Vice-Chancellor Professor Nicola Phillips said changes to migration policy had "created a challenging financial situation that we need to negotiate over the next few years".

"We're starting in an advantageous position," Professor Phillips said.

"But please don't underestimate how carefully we're going to need to manage costs for the foreseeable future, so that we can continue investing in our people and what matters most for our university.

"I repeat my reassurance that we are not considering any radical restructuring of our workforce or our university as a part of our path forward.

" That doesn't mean no change though, and I want to be clear about that. "

Do you know more about this story? Get in touch with Thomas Kelsall at thomaskelsall@proton.me

No forced redundancies promise remains, uni says

The retirement scheme is the latest indicator of financial troubles at the merger university, which opened in January backed by a $464.5 million package from the Malinauskas government.

Adelaide University opened in January 2026 after around three years of transition from its predecessor institutions. (ABC News: Guido Salazar)

The two predecessor institutions, the University of Adelaide and University of South Australia, had promised staff there would be "no compulsory redundancies or retrenchments as a consequence of creating the new institution" until mid-2027.

In response to questions from the ABC, the university did not indicate how many staff it hoped to shed via the early retirement scheme, but said it remained committed to its pre-merger promise.

"University staff have been reassured that we are not considering compulsory redundancies as part of our path forward following the expiry of the employment guarantee in mid-2027," Ms Fox said in a statement.

The voluntary retirement scheme appeared to have the backing of the National Tertiary Education Union.

The union's Adelaide University branch co-president, Associate Professor Virginie Masson, said management was "trying really hard to manage a delicate situation in a way that is not breaking any promise".

"This is a good way to address the issue without forcing people out of a job," she said.

"I think that some people may decide to get their retirement a bit forward because of the stress of the merger — it is very difficult at the moment with the workload."

Adelaide University did not indicate how many staff it hoped to shed via the early retirement scheme. (ABC News: Briana Fiore)

Associate Professor Masson said a problem with the merger was it was "expected that we would have doubling up of the workforce in some areas".

"It was obvious that they will have to take action to try to manage the sheer number of people coming together to work at the university," she said.

The two universities previously said their combined number of academic and professional staff was around 11,000 people.

Government positive about merger

State Development Minister Chris Picton said the university was taking a "sensible approach".

"This is about planning for their workforce and about encouraging and asking people if they are interested in talking about early retirements," he said.

Chris Picton remains positive about the merger. (ABC News: Briana Fiore)

He added there was "no doubt" that the international student decline had been an issue for the institution's financial situation but the government continued to support the merger, which it believed would "pay off in spades" in the long-term.

"We continue to encourage the federal government to support international students because we think that they play an important role for the economy overall," Mr Picton said.

Expressions of interest for the early retirement scheme will close on October 27, the university said in its email to staff. The scheme still needs final approval from the ATO and vice-chancellor.

According to documents seen by the ABC, successful applicants are expected to leave the university by March 31 next year unless an exemption is granted.

No participant will remain beyond June 30, 2027, the documents state, due to the ATO's requirements for the scheme.

title: New law to force Darwin Private Hospital operators to provide maternity care
text:
Chief Minister Lia Finocchiaro says all future operators of the Darwin Private Hospital will be required to provide private maternity services under a new government mandate — but one critic says it could take years to get a new ward up and running.

Calvary Health Care is expected to take over the private hospital before the end of the year after Healthscope shut down the private maternity ward, blaming declining birth rates, and went into receivership last year.

On Thursday, Ms Finocchiaro said while the transition may take time, Calvary and any future operator of Darwin Private Hospital would be required to provide a full maternity service, including private obstetricians and midwifery care.

She dismissed concerns the new policy could discourage private providers from taking over the hospital and would not commit to the government stepping in if birth rates, soaring operational costs and staff shortages once again become a burden.

Chief Minister Lia Finocchiaro says the new legislation will protect families from losing key services in the future. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

"Calvary have just been picked by the receivers as a strong choice to run this hospital," she said.

"They have to have done their homework to be able to stump up and say that they can deliver the services.

"What we're doing is saying, 'you are not welcome here unless you deliver maternity', and as I said, they've already indicated their willingness to do that."

NT's last private obstetrician walks away as maternity services face collapse A growing number of women in the Northern Territory are travelling interstate to give birth — or leaving the territory altogether — following the sudden closure of the only private hospital maternity ward. Now, the NT's last private obstetrician is closing her practice.

Jenny Mitchell, who worked as an obstetrician at the Darwin Private Hospital for 28 years, welcomed the government taking steps to provide certainty for the future, but said rebuilding a ward would take at least two years.

"It's not just obstetricians that we need in the private hospital, we need paediatricians to cover the babies, we need the anaesthetist to provide a 24-hour roster," she told 105.7 ABC Darwin.

"There's no equipment anymore, it's all gone. There are no midwives, there's no nursery nurses.

"So I'm not sure where the government thinks that Calvary is going to pull these people out to get a maternity service running."

The closure of Healthscope's Darwin private maternity ward follows a nationwide decline in maternity services, which obstetricians have described as an "absolute crisis".

Dr Mitchell said Calvary would also be facing a number of challenges threatening its survival of a new ward, including rising costs of private care and private insurance.

"There were 380 deliveries in 2024 and before that when I first started it was like 800 or 900 deliveries [a year]," she said.

Sophia Emberson-Bain, co-lead of Our Birth Our Voice, has been advocating for better access to maternity services for over a year. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

Maternity advocacy group Our Birth, Our Voice organiser Sophia Emberson-Bain said the decision was a "big win" for Territory families.

"It's something that we've actually as a group been calling for from the day that it was announced that Healthscope was dismantling private maternity services," she said.

The legislation is expected to be tabled in parliament next week.

title: How Sally Rooney's support for Palestine Action led to UK exit
text:
Sally Rooney, Ireland's premier voice of sad-girl fiction, can no longer sell her novels in the UK.

Rooney said she was being forced to withdraw her books due to her support for the organisation Palestine Action.

This includes cultural juggernaut Normal People, which has sold more than three million copies.

It is the latest stand-off between those who support the organisation and the UK, which has designated it as a terrorist organisation.

Who is Sally Rooney?

Hailed as the "Salinger for the Snapchat generation", Rooney rose to prominence with 2018's Normal People.

The bestseller was adapted for TV in 2020, starring Paul Mescal in his breakout role, with a series which has been streamed more than 65 million times and broke BBC streaming records that year.

Normal People became a smash hit. (Supplied: Stan)

She was named among Time Magazine's 100 most influential people of 2022, cited by Girls creator Lena Dunham as "the minimalist examiner of modern romance".

Other novels, Conversations with Friends and Intermezzo, achieved similar acclaim.

She has recently become an outspoken voice for Palestine Action, sometimes causing direct conflict with her literary career.

Rooney won the Sky Arts award for literature for Intermezzo last year but did not attend the ceremony, saying she could "no longer safely enter the UK" without potentially facing arrest.

In August, she said she intended to use her novel proceeds and TV residuals to fund Palestine Action.

On Thursday, her publishing house Faber confirmed it "cannot pass on UK earnings".

"As such, and in full agreement with Sally, we have taken the decision that we can no longer supply her works in the UK in any format," it said.

This move will not affect Australian sales.

In a statement to The Guardian, Rooney said it was a result of an op-ed supporting Palestine Action.

The August 2025 piece in The Irish Times outlined her support of the group: "If this makes me a 'supporter of terror' under UK law, so be it."

Sally Rooney (centre) and her hit Normal People helped create the careers of Paul Mescal and Daisy Edgar Jones. (AP: Richard Shotwell/Invision/File)

Who is Palestine Action?

Palestine Action was formed in 2020 by Huda Ammori, and was founded on principles similar to Extinction Rebellion.

It describes itself as a "direct action movement committed to ending global participation in Israel's genocidal and apartheid regime".

This has included attempts to disrupt the supply chains of arms manufacturers Elbit Systems and Lockheed Martin.

In 2022, a protest at a Glasgow weapons equipment factory caused more than £1 million ($1.8 million) in damages.

Palestine Action voices its opposition to Elbit Systems, which is Israeli-founded. (Reuters: Jaimi Joy)

The group's efforts have ramped up since the Gaza War, and the UK has designated it illegal, banning the group under anti-terror legislation.

The US has also imposed sanctions on Palestine Action.

Australia doesn't list the group as a terror organisation, though a 2025 petition was placed before Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke to consider it.

Thousands of protesters have been arrested since the ban on Palestine Action was implemented. (Reuters: Temilade Adelaja)

Palestine Action's ban

The group is legally considered among the likes of ISIS and Al-Qaeda in the UK, and even those wearing a T-shirt supporting the group could face jail time.

More than 3,700 people are believed to have been arrested in relation to the ban, the BBC says.

It is a ban labelled by UN Human Rights Chief Volker Türk as "disproportionate and unnecessary".

"The decision also conflates protected expression and other conduct with acts of terrorism and so could readily lead to further chilling effect on the lawful exercise of these rights by many people," he said.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has defended the ban, saying "supporting the Palestinian cause is not the same as supporting Palestine Action".

Why UK police arrested 466 people for backing a banned pro-Palestine group The Met Police said the 466 arrests for supporting a proscribed organisation were the most made on a single day in the past decade.

It has also faced several legal challenges as seen below:

June 2025: Palestine Action members break into a RAF base in Oxfordshire and spray-paint two military planes red

July 2025: Palestine Action ban comes into effect

February 2026: UK's High Court rules the Home Office's decision unlawful

June 2026: Five Court of Appeal judges rule the government's terror listing is lawful, overruling the High Court decision

June 2026: Four Palestine Action activists are jailed in the first convictions believed to be connected to the terrorism ruling

November 2026 (TBC): Palestine Action to appeal that ruling, with the case to be brought before the UK's highest court next month

The response so far

British Labour MP John McDonnell decried the move, saying he was "really worried people will be deprived of the opportunity of listening to Sally Rooney's words".

"If a great Irish writer's books can no longer be published in the UK because she stands with Palestine, the question isn't what law might Sally Rooney have broken, it's what sort of country has Britain become," Patrick Corrigan, head of nations and regions at Amnesty International UK, said.

Readers and Writers Against the Genocide co-founder Kirsty Wilson said it also left questions about who in the UK would want to acquire Rooney's next book.

"Perhaps she will publish with an Irish publisher, and a local Australian publisher etc. and bypass the UK for now," she said.

More broadly, Wilson said it was reflective of the issues pro-Palestinian Australian authors also faced.

She pointed to author Randa Abdel-Fattah, who was uninvited from the Adelaide Writers' Festival, with the then-board claiming it would be "culturally insensitive" for her to appear due to past statements she had made regarding Israel and Zionism.

An Indigenous author's picture book was also scrapped for publication in April after past comments by illustrator Matt Chun were found to have breached the University of Queensland's policy on antisemitism.

"Palestinian Australian writers and pro-Palestinian writers are definitely experiencing free speech concerns whenever they advocate for Palestine . These voices are being silenced and there is a definite chilling effect," Wilson said.

title: Wallabies show faith in rookie fly half for final All Blacks Test
text:
Declan Meredith will start at fly half against the All Blacks for just the fourth time in his young Test career, as the Wallabies make changes for Saturday's final Bledisloe Cup clash at Sydney's Stadium Australia.

Meredith, who made his Test debut against France in July, replaces Ben Donaldson in the number 10 jersey.

Donaldson was ruled out with a minor upper leg injury in the wake of the 50-19 thrashing dished out by the All Blacks at Auckland's Eden Park last Saturday night.

Back-up fly half Harry McLaughlin-Phillips will make his Test debut if he comes on as a reserve in Sydney.

He is joined on the bench by reserve scrum half Kalani Thomas, who is yet to play a Bledisloe Cup Test.

Wallabies thrashed by All Blacks The Wallabies are outclassed by a rampant All Blacks outfit at Eden Park, with the home side retaining the Bledisloe Cup for yet another year.

It will be a tough initiation for Meredith, although he will be playing outside Brumbies teammate and scrum half, Ryan Lonergan.

The 27-year-old got his first taste of playing the All Blacks after coming on as a reserve at Eden Park last weekend.

Meanwhile, the Wallabies have moved Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii back to the centres.

He started on the wing in the Wallabies' past two Tests, but the absence of Len Ikitau (concussion) forced Wallabies coach Les Kiss to shift the ex-NRL star back to the midfield.

He will partner Isaac Henry, who switches from outside to inside centre, while Harry Potter will start on the wing.

Ikitau is a massive loss for the Wallabies, who are also missing Hunter Paisami (suspension) from their midfield options.

Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii has been shifted back to the centres for the Wallabies. (Getty Images: Brendon Thorne)

Elsewhere in the Wallabies' match-day squad, former All Black Aidan Ross will start at loosehead prop, alongside hooker Josh Nasser.

Ross replaces Angus Bell, while Brandon Paenga-Amosa (rested) made way for Nasser.

Hooker Billy Pollard, lock Josh Canham, openside flanker Carlo Tizzano and utility back Filipo Daugunu have returned to the Wallabies' squad as reserves.

Wallaroos lose star for historic 'quadruple header' The Wallaroos are forced to reshuffle their backline for Saturday's Test against Scotland at Sydney's Stadium Australia.

"We got a clear picture last weekend of where we need to be better," Kiss said in a Rugby Australia statement.

"We've said all along we'll continue to work hard and grow our game, and the squad has been impressive in the way they have prepared this week."

Lukhan Salakaia-Loto, who retained his place alongside Jeremy Williams in the second row, will appear in his 50th Test.

The Bledisloe Cup Test will cap off a historic "quadruple header" at Stadium Australia.

The Wallaroos play Scotland earlier in the day, while the Australian women's and men's sevens teams meet New Zealand and Fiji respectively.

It is the first time all four national teams have featured on the same match-day schedule.

Wallabies squad (1-15): Aidan Ross, Josh Nasser, Allan Alaalatoa, Jeremy Williams, Lukhan Salakaia-Loto, Rob Valetini, Fraser McReight, Harry Wilson, Ryan Lonergan, Declan Meredith, Harry Potter, Isaac Henry, Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii, Max Jorgensen, Tom Wright

Reserves: Billy Pollard, Angus Bell, Massimo De Lutiis, Josh Canham, Carlo Tizzano, Kalani Thomas, Harry McLaughlin-Phillips, Filipo Daugunu

title: Industrial relations minister could terminate strikes under proposed Qld laws
text:
Queensland's industrial relations minister would have the power to terminate protected industrial action in certain circumstances, under new proposed laws.

Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie has introduced sweeping changes to the state's industrial relations laws that he said "mirrored as much as possible the Fair Work legislation".

This year Queensland Rail and seven unions spent months negotiating in the Fair Work Commission with protected industrial action and a maintenance backlog resulting in reduced services and frequent delays for commuters.

Mr Bleijie said he wrote to the federal industrial relations minister to intervene.

"There was some militancy there," he said.

He said if the rail situation was a "state rail issue" and not under the Fair Work legislation, he suspected the state government would have "absolutely" intervened.

Jarrod Bleijie said the proposed laws "essentially mimicked" federal laws introduced by Julia Gillard's government in 2009. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

"There was too much disruption to commuters," Mr Bleijie, who also serves as the Industrial Relations Minister, said.

He said the proposed laws "essentially mimicked" federal laws introduced by Julia Gillard's government in 2009.

"But these laws are used in very limited circumstances … it would be extraordinary situations," Mr Bleijie said.

Three days' notice for strikes

Under the proposed changes, the minister could terminate protected industrial action if satisfied there is a sufficient public interest justification.

Protected industrial action could be terminated if it would threaten to endanger the life, personal safety, health or welfare or cause significant damage to the state's economy.

Qld industrial relations review 104 recommendations A review of Queensland's industrial relations laws has handed down its report.

The bill would also require at least three working days' notice for protected industrial action.

"The striking ability is still there. We've kept arbitration. We've kept conciliation," Mr Bleijie said.

The state's industrial relations jurisdiction covers around 383,000 workers. The remaining estimated 2.66 million workers are covered by the Fair Work Act 2009.

The legislation followed an independent review of the state's industrial relations laws.

The reviewers received written submissions from 97 stakeholders, representing employers, unions, workers, insurers and other key interest groups.

The report made 104 recommendations, and the state government accepted 75 of them in full.

The proposed changes would also require employment to be the "major significant" contributing factor for psychological injury claims.

"Over the past decade, the number of accepted psychological injury claims has increased by almost 268 per cent, including an increase of more than 76 per cent over the past five years alone," Mr Bleijie told state parliament on Wednesday night.

Queensland's peak union body said proposed changes would make it harder for frontline workers to access support for psychological injuries.

Queensland Council of Unions General Secretary Jacqueline King said psychological injuries can have more than one cause.

Jacqueline King said these changes "should not be rushed through parliament". (ABC News: Rachel Riga)

"Requiring work to be the major contributing factor risks shutting workers out of compensation and access to the support they need," she said.

"These changes should not be rushed through parliament with all stakeholders needing sufficient time to consult and scrutinise their impact."

The bill has been referred to a parliamentary committee for examination before it is brought back for debate in the House.

title: 'Not a lot we can do': Yass council region faces 76pc rate hike
text:
Residents in Yass, Murrumbateman and Sutton are facing a 76 per cent increase in their rates, following a Yass Valley Council decision to take the measure to public consultation.

The motion passed 5-4 after the council called an extraordinary meeting on Wednesday to address its financial issues.

Independent consultants have found the council would need to generate an extra $8.3 million from operations each year by 2027-28 to maintain its financial and infrastructure position.

The council has put a special rate variation to the community for feedback. (ABC News)

The motion means the council will spend six weeks in community consultation, taking three financial options to the public.

All three would result in a cumulative 76 per cent increase in rates, but the different models would stage the increases differently over the four years.

Mayor Jasmin Jones stressed this did not mean council had decided to approve the rate hike.

"It was a decision to go out to our community for the next six weeks to put our boots on the ground, to get that really robust feedback from our community," she said.

Mayor says 'structural problem' with NSW council funding

Ultimately the council would also need the special rate variation to be approved by the NSW Independent Pricing and Regulatory Tribunal.

Speaking to 666 ABC Canberra, Cr Jones agreed 76 per cent sounded like "a lot".

"But that is the structural financial correction that is happening across New South Wales right now," she said.

" Yass Valley Council is certainly not alone in the need to go for a special rate variation at least once every 10 years. "

Yass Valley Council mayor Jasmin Jones has defended its financial management. (ABC News: Simon Beardsell)

She pushed back against suggestions the council had mismanaged its finances.

"I think it's fair to say that if every rural council is going for a special rate variation every 10 years, that tells you that there's a structural problem in how councils are funded," she said.

"Our rate peg only allows us to put up rates every year — for example, 3.4 per cent or 3.7 or 3.9 — when the cost of materials skyrocketed, for example, during the diesel crisis."

Asked about the decision to invest in a new council building, which has drawn some ire in the community, Cr Jones said it had been necessary.

"The workplace wasn't fit for purpose — we had people's chairs actually falling through the floor, it was beyond redeeming that particular building," she said.

Cr Jones also conceded they were struggling to keep up with roads maintenance.

"I can totally accept that in terms of roads, that when we say we're going to come and grade that road three times a year and we're struggling to do even once, that they'd be dissatisfied," she said.

The extraordinary meeting led to a vote to put the three financial options to the public. (ABC News: Simon Beardsell)

'There's not a lot that we can do'

The near three-hour meeting was passionate at times with members of the public having their say.

Malcolm Bamford, who lives in the council area, said he did not feel confident after leaving the meeting.

"The decision had to be made, OK, but the biggest concern ... was how are they going to do it?" he said.

"They've got an increase before, and then we've another one, nothing really came out of it that makes you confident.

"If we need the money, there's not a lot that we can do.

"We've got to get out of the trouble that we're in."

Yass Valley Council chief executive Gayleen Burley said it was an "emotive" issue for people struggling to keep up with costs.

"We have compassionate debt recovery services," she said.

"But also we want to engage early with our residents, so that if there is an issue with meeting the demand for an increase in rates, that they're able to engage with council and we can come to a workable solution."

Yass Valley Council chief executive Gayleen Burley says compassionate financial assistance is available. (ABC News: Simon Beardsell)

Renters urged to have their say too

The issue of financial sustainability in local government is not new, and a federal inquiry into their viability is currently underway.

In 2024, the Australian Local Government Association (ALGA) called for a greater cut of federal tax revenue.

In November last year, the Yass Valley Council deferred a vote on a rate increase of between 40 and 58 per cent.

Cr Jones urged all residents to have their say on the proposal.

She said the variation would not apply to services such as rubbish collection, water or sewerage.

"And I just want to emphasise that everyone can have a say, you don't need to be receiving a rates bill to have a say on this.

"So if you're a renter, we still need to hear from you because these are costs that get passed on to you.

"We need to hear from community and sporting organisations, young people, families, older residents across not just Yass and Murrumbateman, but also our villages."

title: Conroy targets 'rot' in Defence after $15.6m bungle unmasked
text:
Defence officials behind Australia's flagship missile program racked up at least $15.6 million in financial and procurement blunders, a freedom of information document shows, including paying out $13.3 million before securing basic legal sign-off.

The defence file exposes a pattern of basic accounting and administrative failures within the Guided Weapons and Explosive Ordnance Group (GWEO), the $36 billion initiative designed to manufacture and stockpile advanced weapons and ammunition on Australian soil.

The federal government acknowledged the errors exposed in the document, with Defence Industry Minister Pat Conroy telling the ABC: "We agree the rot has to stop."

The defence document shows the administrative errors included two payments of $8.1 million and $5.2 million, which were made in June 2023.

Officials paid out the money to cover contract price hikes before getting the mandatory legal approval required to increase the contract's value.

A further four transactions broke basic rules when staff went out to market to get quotes before getting required sign-off from their managers.

In another instance, officials broke spending rules on a $631,365 order by approving a bill that was higher than the allowed spending limit, then mistakenly filing the paperwork in Australian dollars instead of the foreign currency, distorting the exchange rate used.

The money represents a tiny fraction of the multi-billion-dollar defence procurement budget but it raises concerns about how the funds are handled.

There is no suggestion any of the money was lost, but Defence records make it clear the funds were spent "contrary to Defence procurement policy".

More breaches redacted from document

An unknown number of additional breaches and their costs were redacted from the document.

However, "yes" boxes confirm corrective action was required on at least eight additional occasions.

The paperwork also highlights broader procedural lapses across the program, including an August 2025 breach where staff relied on outdated spending rules, missing a policy change that dropped the manager sign-off threshold from $200,000 to $80,000.

Pat Conroy and South Australian Premier Peter Malinauskas pictured last year touring a missile assembly factory. (Supplied: Defence/Kym Smith)

The errors were only identified when a new contract management team conducted a review of previous transactions.

"The personnel involved in processing the escalation payment are no longer within the Contract Management Team," the Defence document said, explaining the current team reviewed the arrangement, identified the non-compliance, and formally reported it.

Officials ultimately granted retrospective approval to the $13.3 million in payments on July 10, 2025, about two years after the cash went out the door.

Do you know more? If you know more about this story, contact Olivia Caisley at oliviacaisley.journo@proton.me

Mr Conroy used the ABC's revelations to justify the Albanese government's creation of the newly minted Defence Delivery Group to improve oversight, enforce tighter controls on contracts and get "more bang for the buck for taxpayers".

He also laid blame at the feet of the former Liberal government.

"The management of this contract, a legacy of the former government that outsourced important work to a legion of consultants and contractors, was just not good enough," he said.

"We agree the rot has to stop. That's why since coming to office, we have acted to ensure that the management of this contract is now done by Defence public servants.

"That's why we have ramped up investment in GWEO and made it a priority, which includes greater oversight of management of this contract."

The FOI document shows the unauthorised price-hike payments occurred in June 2023, more than a year after the Albanese government first took office.

Greens want accountability

Greens leader David Shoebridge, who is also the party's spokesperson on defence, said the issue highlighted deep issues with defence procurement.

"GWEO is one of the government's big-ticket items on defence spending. Questions need to be asked about who was held to account here," he said.

"The documents only say the 'personnel involved' have been moved on.

"In most cases in Defence, 'moved on' is code for promoted away from a problem.

"What is 100 per cent clear is that no-one in a leadership position has even been held to account."

David Shoebridge says Defence should not "promote away the problem". (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

A Defence spokesperson told the ABC the department took issues of non-compliance and transparency seriously.

"[It has] demonstrated this through proactive referrals, stronger controls, and increased oversight," they said.

Audit office looks into domestic munitions

The internal disclosures come amid an extensive, two-part investigation by the Australian National Audit Office (ANAO) into Defence's domestic munitions contracts.

The national audit body first exposed severe probity gaps and sole-sourcing failures in June 2024, before handing down a damning second report in July 2026 that criticised the GWEO enterprise for delivering "limited assurance" on value-for-money.

The GWEO division will be consolidated into the new Defence Delivery Agency. (Supplied: Defence/Rodney Braithwaite)

The government has committed between $26 billion and $36 billion over the next decade under the Integrated Investment Program to accelerate the GWEO enterprise.

GWEO is among the divisions set to be consolidated into the new Defence Delivery Agency, which will manage Australia's $56 billion annual defence spending from July 2027.

The initiative aims to curb costly project blowouts on major military assets.

title: Unemployment at five-year high after nearly 40,000 jobs lost
text:
Australia's unemployment rate remained at 4.7 per cent in September, after August's jobless rate was revised upwards.

It means the national unemployment rate remains at its highest level in the post-COVID era, in seasonally adjusted terms.

An estimated 39,300 fewer Australians were in work last month, and the number of officially unemployed people increased by 8,900.

Inflation lower than expected The odds of the Reserve Bank lifting interest rates in November have fallen sharply after the latest consumer price index (CPI) came in lower than expected, with headline inflation up 4 per cent in the year to August.

The participation rate, which is the proportion of people in work or actively looking for work, also fell, to 66.8 per cent from 67 per cent.

It means the average unemployment rate in the September quarter was 4.63 per cent, well above (and ahead of) the Reserve Bank's forecast of 4.5 per cent for the December quarter this year.

The Bureau of Statistics data show that, in trend terms, things remained steady last month.

The trend unemployment rate remained at 4.6 per cent (with no upward revision), the participation rate held at 66.9 per cent, hours worked remained steady, and the employment-to-population ratio held at 63.8 per cent.

Unemployment will keep rising

Tom Kennedy from JP Morgan said the unemployment rate had now increased by 0.6 percentage points since the RBA started lifting interest rates in February.

He said outside of the COVID-19-related volatility, it was the largest nine-month increase in more than a decade.

RBA hikes interest rates to 4.6pc The Reserve Bank increases interest rates to 4.6 per cent in its fourth rate rise this year.

"The deterioration is also more pronounced than the RBA had forecast back in August, with the Statement on Monetary Policy projecting an unemployment rate of 4.5 per cent by year-end," he said.

"Importantly, it's too early to see any effect from the RBA's September rate hike, which we think will weigh on both GDP growth and labour demand in coming quarters."

Oxford Economics Australia economist Oscar Guth said unemployment would keep rising over the next 12 months.

He expects the unemployment rate to exceed 4.8 per cent late in 2027 as the lagged effects of oil price shocks and tighter monetary policy continue to affect the labour market.

BDO chief economist Anders Magnusson said the RBA's restrictive monetary policy and slow economic growth were beginning to flow more clearly into the labour market.

"The result suggests that the labour market is moving further in the direction the Reserve Bank has been seeking," he said.

RBA November meeting is still 'live'

Despite the clear signs that labour market conditions are still loosening, some economists think the RBA may soon lift rates again.

EY senior economist Paula Gadsby said today's data had not changed the monetary policy outlook.

Climate change and corruption are also driving up interest rates Typically, bond rates rise when an economy is doing well and inflation appears to be moving up. But something much deeper and more structural is currently going on.

"Given persistent price pressures across the economy, we continue to expect at least one rate hike before the end of the year, potentially as soon as Melbourne Cup Day," she said.

CBA economist Ashwin Clarke said next month's RBA Monetary Policy Board meeting would be closely watched.

"The data suggests the labour market continues to gradually loosen," he said.

"On the margin, this supports our expectation that the RBA will hold interest rates steady at its November meeting, though risks remain firmly tilted to the upside and the meeting is live."

Westpac's economics team still expect a rate hike in November.

David Bassanese, BetaShares chief economist, said he also thought the RBA would lift rates in November, but that decision would hinge on an "all-important inflation reading" later this month.

But Tom Kennedy said he thought rates would probably be on hold for a while.

"While price pressures are still elevated and the RBA remains focused on inflation, the steady increase in the jobless rate, in our view, argues for a period of policy stability and we expect rates on hold from here," he said.

title: Wallaroos lose star but regain experience for historic 'quadruple header'
text:
The Wallaroos have been forced to leave out star fullback Caitlyn Halse for Saturday's Test against Scotland at Sydney's Stadium Australia.

Halse is unavailable for the WXV Global Series Test due to concussion symptoms.

The 20-year-old's withdrawal is a blow but the Wallaroos have regained experienced winger Maya Stewart, who returns to the starting XV.

Stewart, a 27-Test veteran with the Wallaroos, was named after recovering from an Achilles tendon injury.

Her inclusion sees Desiree Miller move from the wing to fullback in place of Halse.

Wallaroos 'got some work to do' Ending a run of six straight defeats was not enough to leave the Wallaroos satisfied with their 30-10 win over Scotland in Edinburgh this morning.

In the forward pack, captain Siokapesi Palu Sekona and Pia Tapsell swap positions in the back row, starting at blindside flanker and number eight respectively.

Eva Karpani and Cecilia Smith have returned to the match-day squad on the reserves bench, which also features fresh faces Allana Sikimeti and Piper Simons.

"We have maintained considerable selection consistency throughout the WXV, strategically strengthening our cohesion and combinations," Rugby Australia's director of women's high performance, Tim Walsh, said in a statement.

"During the WXV we have layered specific areas of our game to build stronger performances each Test.

"We have selected a balanced 23 armed with leadership, power, strength and speed."

Wallaroos captain Siokapesi Palu Sekona will play at blindside flanker against Scotland. (Getty Images: Mark Nolan)

The Wallaroos are chasing back-to-back wins over Scotland.

In their most recent Test, the Wallaroos triumphed 30–10 in Edinburgh late last month.

The two sides meet in Sydney and Canberra (October 23) to conclude their WXV Global Series campaigns.

Saturday's match is part of a rugby "quadruple header" at Stadium Australia.

The Wallabies meet the All Blacks in the final Bledisloe Cup Test, while the Australian women's and men's sevens teams are also appearing.

The world champion Australian women's team plays arch rivals New Zealand, while the men's squad faces two-time Olympic champions Fiji.

It is the first time all four national rugby teams will be playing on the same match-day schedule.

title: Patients struggling with rising costs and long waits for healthcare refunds
text:
Victoria's Labor government and the opposition have promised $53.6 million for the Victorian Patient Transport Assistance Scheme (VPTAS) if successful at next month's state election.

The scheme provides financial assistance to eligible Victorians who need to travel long distances to access specialist medical treatment.

Under proposed changes to the program, accommodation subsidies would increase from $45 to $125 a night and fuel reimbursements from 21 cents per kilometre to 35 cents.

Mildura woman Lara Hamilton is one of almost 30,000 regional Victorians who use the VPTAS.

She regularly visits Melbourne for appointments and mostly relies on flights for her travel.

Lara Hamilton uses a mobility scooter and relies on flights and one-way lifts from family members. (ABC News: Wade Stephens)

She called the announcement a "bandaid" solution and said her budget would still be tight, as reimbursements could take months to hit her account.

Currently, she is waiting on claims for thousands of dollars.

"With the cost-of-living crisis at the moment, no-one can afford to wait for $4,500," she said.

"I have to choose to basically not drive my own motor vehicle locally to try to save money, catch a bus or walk when I can."

The standard processing time for a claim is six to eight weeks, but Ms Hamilton said she had been waiting much longer.

"I lodge paper forms and it's taking an excess of six months for any type of reimbursement," she said.

"If you're lucky, you may receive an email approximately four months post-lodgement."

'Impossible' wait times

Mildura couple Wendy and Eddie Rushforth access VPTAS to cover the cost of travel for medical treatment across the state.

Ms Rushforth said the couple had also cut back on their spending to save up for appointments.

"[We] cut down on our food, turn everything off for the electricity and don't drive anywhere," she said.

Ed and Wendy Rushforth have to budget to afford travel to doctor and specialist appointments. (ABC News: Wade Stephens)

Ms Rushforth said even the estimated wait times were too long.

"Six to eight weeks is a long time without having money, and to not be able to shop because you have to save up for so long," she said.

Funding increase

To access the scheme, Australian citizens, permanent residents or refugees must travel 100 kilometres one way or 500km within seven days.

The service must be from the closest eligible specialist service.

Ingrid Stitt says the increase will make a "real difference". (ABC News)

"We don't want people to have to worry about money as well as everything else that they're dealing with," Health Minister Ingrid Stitt said.

Ms Stitt said the government had introduced measures to decrease wait times, including the launch of an online portal.

"We've also put some additional resources into the team that processes those claims because we do want to see people get reimbursed a lot quicker," she said.

Not-for-profit organisation Sunraysia Cancer Resources covers travel costs for north-west Victorian clients and submits reimbursement through VPTAS.

Manager Bronwyn Lockwood said the group was owed almost $300,000 from the scheme at one point, but on the past week, a number of payments had been received.

"We are very grateful for the efforts that are being made to process the claims," she said.

End of 'postcode penalty'

Georgie Crozier says the Coalition has been advocating for an increase to accommodation and petrol reimbursement rates. (AAP: James Ross)

Shadow Health Minister Georgie Crozier said Labor had 12 years to fix issues with VPTAS yet waited until a few weeks out from the election.

"The Coalition has long been advocating on behalf of regional Victorians for an increase in the accommodation and petrol rates under the VPTAS, which are the lowest in the country under Labor," Ms Crozier said.

According to the Leukaemia Foundation's National Patient Travel Scorecard, Victoria has the worst reimbursement options in the country.

Under the new funding, Victoria would move to equal first alongside South Australia.

Chris Tanti says the foundation's focus will now turn to how the funding is delivered. (ABC News)

"Victorians facing cancer [treatment] now have something they have not had before: a clear, costed promise to end the postcode penalty," CEO Chris Tanti said.

Mr Tanti said bipartisan support was a "significant milestone", but it had come after more than a decade of pushing for change.

The funding change is expected to roll out on July 1, 2027, if either Labor or the Coalition forms government.

title: Brisbane City Council floats trialling licensed bars on CityCats
text:
Brisbane's CityCats could soon become floating bars, with the council exploring options to add alcohol licensing to the city's ferries.

Brisbane City Council (BCC) has confirmed it is looking into a pilot program that would see ten double-decker CityCat ferries outfitted with licensed bars.

Councillor Andrew Wines told ABC Radio Brisbane the plan was in its early stages.

"We're having a look at an idea where … we can have a food and beverage offering on our ferries to allow people the option to be able to buy a drink if they wish on the ferry on the way home," he said.

BCC says the idea was inspired by Sydney ferry services that serve alcohol, such as the Manly Ferry. (ABC News: Dean Caton)

Lord mayor Adrian Schrinner said Brisbane needed to be a city that "says yes to things".

"All I'm saying is let's give it a go. Let's see if it works," Cr Schrinner said.

"Let's see how the community responds; if they love it, we'll keep doing it, if they don't love it, we'll stop doing it.

"It's as simple as that."

Adrian Schrinner says Brisbane should be a city that "says yes to things". (ABC News: Lucas Hill)

He said he would like to see the trial up and running next year.

"I think this is something that we'd like to see if it works quickly," he said.

The idea has drawn some criticism from local residents, with one caller describing it as "a ridiculous idea".

"What's next, beers on the bus?" Gavin said.

"You've got families using those things, kids there. People are going to get intoxicated.

" What happens if they have an accident because they're drunk and they slip getting off the ferry? "

Cr Wines said BCC would take licensing requirements into account, including serving food and practising responsible service of alcohol.

"This is not going to be a party boat, this is going to be an opportunity to have a drink here and there, not dissimilar to Straddie … and not dissimilar to Manly Ferry in Sydney," he said.

Cr Wines says licensing laws would be taken into account, including serving food and practising responsible service of alcohol. (ABC News)

He said matters like opening hours and product offerings were still being worked through.

Deputy leader of the Labor council opposition Lucy Collier said the council had the "wrong priorities".

"Brisbane's LNP Lord Mayor thinks it's fine for CityCat staff to be overworked and underpaid, and now he wants them to become bartenders and clean up intoxicated people's vomit," Cr Collier said.

Pay negotiations still ongoing

The plan comes at a fraught moment for CityCat operator RiverCity Ferries, which is still working through a new pay deal with Brisbane ferry staff.

Pay negotiations between MUA and the operator have been ongoing since October last year, with workers conducting industrial action intermittently since July 30.

In a statement, the MUA and the Australian Maritime Officers Union (AMOU) said the idea "doesn't pass the pub test".

Brisbane ferry workers to strike on Riverfire Brisbane ferry workers have been undertaking intermittent industrial action since July 30, with pay negotiations between the Maritime Union of Australia and RiverCity Ferries stalling.

"Our members already deal with unruly and intoxicated passengers on late-night services," said MUA Queensland secretary Aaron Johnston.

"Putting alcohol on board will make that worse and add workload and risk for crew whose first job is the safety of everyone on a moving vessel."

AMOU industrial officer Tracey Ellis said CityCats did not have enough power available to run the required refrigerators, among other issues.

"I bet there has been no stability calculations done to see if the CityCats can even carry the extra weight of a bar and drinks, let-a-lone a risk assessment on how they are going to deal with an emergency with less room to move with all the extra equipment and drunk passengers," Ms Ellis said.

Cr Wines said he wasn't certain how pay negotiations were progressing.

"I believe that negotiations have been progressing and that the two groups … my understanding is that things have been improving and I remain optimistic."

title: Surge in iron infusions prompts warning over serious side effect
text:
Kate Russell thought getting an iron infusion would help alleviate her fatigue, but she says the treatment instead led to a condition that landed her in an induced coma.

The 46-year-old said she was not warned about the potential risks and the 12 months since her admission to Toowoomba Hospital's intensive care unit (ICU) had been "devastating".

Ms Russell said she was diagnosed with severe hypophosphataemia – dangerously low phosphate in the blood – which can occur after an iron infusion.

"[I had] countless specialist appointments and medications, as well as using up all my personal leave and having to give up parts of my role [as a teacher]," she said.

"It's taken a huge financial toll on my family."

Kate Russell says she was active before getting an iron infusion. (Supplied: Kate Russell)

She said the only risk associated with an iron infusion she was told about was iron staining on her arm where the intravenous needle was inserted.

But Ms Russell said she started experiencing muscle weakness and heart palpitations after her treatment in October last year, and she continued to deteriorate for a month before she collapsed in a doctor's surgery and was rushed to hospital.

"I just could not continue to breathe, so they decided that they needed to take over my breathing and intubate me," she said.

She said when the cause of her illness was identified, she was given phosphate replacement therapy.

Iron infusion risk becoming more common

Women of reproductive age are getting iron infusions at an increasingly high rate. (ABC: Emily Bryan)

Medical experts say hypophosphataemia is a complication that can occur with the use of ferric carboxymaltose, an intravenous iron preparation commonly administered in Australia.

Recent data shows it is becoming more common as iron infusions surge across Australia, particularly among women of reproductive age.

There were 46 reports of hypophosphataemia associated with ferric carboxymaltose in 2025, compared with 17 cases in 2020 according to the Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA).

Bond University assistant professor and general practitioner Kieran Le Plastrier said several patients had presented to his practice feeling "generally unwell" after receiving iron infusions this year and blood tests had shown they all had low phosphate.

Hypophosphataemia is becoming more common as the use of iron infusions rises. (Supplied: Queensland Health)

"They felt really, really terrible at a time when they're expecting to feel really great because we've done the iron infusion," he said.

Dr Le Plastrier said ferric carboxymaltose caused hypophosphataemia by preventing the breakdown of a hormone, which in turn signalled the kidneys to excrete more phosphate than usual.

"All versions of infusions can do it, but this particular product has a high rate because it blocks the conversion of certain cofactors in the gut and in the blood from being able to recycle and absorb phosphate," he said.

"Phosphate turns over every day; we excrete it in our kidneys and in our stool and this product can actually cause that to increase significantly."

He said patients experiencing low phosphate levels were treated with an oral replacement and usually returned to regular health within a few months in mild cases.

Kieran Le Plastrier says iron infusions can cause the kidneys to waste phosphate. (ABC Gold Coast: Danielle Mahe)

US strengthens warnings

Last month, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) brought in its strongest safety warning, a boxed warning, for ferric carboxymaltose due to the risks of hypophosphataemia.

The Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) said it was "aware of and currently evaluating" the move in the United States, but did not say whether Australia would adopt the same warning.

The organisation said it routinely monitored safety information and added that action taken by overseas regulators did not automatically result in the same action in Australia.

Royal Australian College of General Practitioners (RACGP) co-deputy chair Aadhil Aziz said Australian regulators should consider following the US to ensure patients and healthcare professionals were better informed about the potential risk.

"Having a warning doesn't mean that you don't do this," Dr Aziz said.

"It just means that you're paying more attention to the phosphate and I don't think that's a bad thing."

He said patients should discuss dietary changes or oral iron tablets with their regular doctor before opting for an iron infusion.

For patients who required intravenous iron, he said checking phosphate levels before treatment could also help identify potential risk factors.

"We want our Australian patients to be safe and by focusing on safety first, making sure that this doesn't happen and what can be prevented is prevented," Dr Aziz said.

Kate Russell urges others to be aware of symptoms. (Supplied: Kate Russell)

Meanwhile, Ms Russell said it had taken her almost a year to recover, and she had only recently returned to work full-time as a physical education teacher.

She urged anyone thinking about getting iron infusions to do their research before getting the treatment.

"Look out for these symptoms post-iron infusion. If you experience it, go straight back to your GP," she said.

"I don't think anyone should have to experience this."

title: Tasmanian premier's school Christmas intervention labelled 'reprehensible'
text:
Tasmanian Premier Jeremy Rockliff is being urged to apologise after one of his social media posts about a public school renaming a Christmas event caused an online stir.

Late on Wednesday night, Mr Rockliff posted on Facebook that he was aware of "efforts made to remove all references to Christmas in end-of-year school celebrations".

"Acknowledging other traditions is important. But that's not a reason to abandon our own," the premier wrote.

"Christmas is a time that brings us together. And our school kids should be encouraged to sing Christmas carols whenever they please.

"I have requested that the education department step in."

The social media post, which has attracted more than 900 comments as of this morning, did not mention a school by name.

However, comments on the premier's post as well as reporting in other media named the school as Trevallyn Primary School, in Launceston, and also named the acting principal.

Many of the comments on the Facebook post were supportive of the premier's statement.

Speaking at a press conference on Thursday, Mr Rockliff did not apologise for the social media post, saying he was "expressing a view in a very measured way".

"I condemn any attack on any individual or any particular school very clearly, and that's not what I've done," he said.

School renames event 'End of Year Extravaganza'

Trevallyn Primary School had plans to rename its Christmas on the Hill event. (ABC News: Georgia Hogge)

In a newsletter to families dated October 2, the school said it was planning for its December fundraising raffle "formerly known as Christmas on the Hill", which it noted was now called the "End of Year Extravaganza!"

The calendar in the same newsletter still makes multiple references to Christmas, including planned Christmas Carols and a "Christmas celebration at Tailrace Park", with an image of a Christmas tree.

A recent school calendar shows references to Christmas. (Supplied)

The premier also yesterday sent a letter to department secretary Ginna Webster naming the school and referencing correspondence he had received from a parent.

"I do not support schools removing reference to Christmas in end-of-year celebrations or removing carols," he wrote.

At the time of writing, the Trevallyn Primary School calendar lists "TPS Christmas Carols" on December 10.

Premier's actions 'reprehensible', union says

Australian Education Union Tasmanian state manager Brian Wightman told 936 ABC Hobart he was appalled by the premier's actions.

"The impact is significant," Mr Wightman said.

"We're talking about one school where now a public servant has been named and the school shamed along with the school association.

" The consequences of this are significant and the psychological harm that the premier has caused is reprehensible. "

Loading...

He said he had yesterday provided the principal's phone number to Mr Rockliff and urged him to make contact and hear the reasons for the school's celebration changes before reacting.

Mr Wightman said the premier should now make that call, apologise and rectify the situation.

"It has been blown out of all proportion. The premier's actions are reprehensible and he must pick up the phone today and fix this," he said.

The premier said there had been "efforts made to remove all references to Christmas in end-of-year school celebrations", which he opposed. (ABC News: Jane Cowan)

Mat Grining, who is president of the Tasmania Principal Association, posted on his personal Facebook page echoing a similar sentiment.

"I'm outraged that the premier thinks this is an appropriate use of his office's time, energy and resources to weigh in on an issue that has already been consulted and led by the parent committee of the school," Mr Grining said.

"This is absolute overreach. Thank you to the parents and families that express their goodwill towards the deeply committed staff in their local communities."

On Thursday, Mr Rockliff said he made the post after "listening to parents" and suggested there were "other examples" of schools removing references to Christmas.

"That's why I've written to the head of the education department with my very clear expectation that Christmas in all our schools is here to stay," he said.

The education department has been contacted for comment.

Education Minister Jo Palmer, who attended the school as a child, has also been contacted for comment.

title: Hundreds of outback burial sites uncovered by Dave 'the Grave' Hunter
text:
The first time Dave Hunter went searching for unmarked graves was as a teenager on his grandfather's farm in Rushworth, northern Victoria.

After being given the task of finding buried bulls on the property, he built a rudimentary "radar" with a multimeter.

He has since found hundreds of graves, most recently in far-west New South Wales.

More than 300 grave sites were identified at the White Cliffs cemetery. (Supplied: Central Darling Shire Council)

In July 2025, the Central Darling Shire Council contracted him to determine whether there were any lost graves in Menindee and White Cliffs.

Using his equipment, he found more than 300 burials in each place, all connected to the existing cemeteries.

Mr Hunter said there was a real sense of satisfaction to see all the markers on the previously lost graves.

"Particularly in Menindee, it was really eye-opening to see so many," he said.

The Central Darling Shire Council wants to identify people in the unmarked graves. (Supplied: Central Darling Shire Council)

Finding those once lost

The council's cemetery officer, Tammie McMaster, is now on a mission to identify the souls beneath the ground.

She has been speaking to locals and scouring council records and archives.

"If I could do the majority [of the graves], just to put a name to these people, [that] would be absolutely fantastic," Ms McMaster said.

The Central Darling Shire has launched a project to identify people buried in unmarked graves. (ABC News: Gavin Coote)

The council is looking at repeating the project in other far-west communities, including in Wilcannia and Tilpa.

Ms McMaster said the project was vital not only for future planning in the cemeteries, but for honouring the dead.

"It's respectful to the people that are laid to rest, and to families and relatives," she said.

Relying on technology

Unmarked graves are common in Australia, as a result of how someone was laid to rest, or records and markers becoming lost to time.

Mr Hunter uses a sophisticated ground-penetrating radar, which looks a bit like a lawn mower, to find lost graves without once ever lifting a shovel.

Dave Hunter completes 10 to 15 projects a year to find unmarked graves at cemeteries. (Supplied: David Hunter)

His radar technology helps him measure electrical resistivity, or disturbances in the soil.

"It's important to note that we're not actually detecting a body as such or any sort of skeletal remains," Mr Hunter said.

"It is literally just the hole that has been dug in the ground that this technology detects."

While it is not an exact science, Mr Hunter takes an educated guess when figuring out whether he has found a grave.

"If we're in a cemetery context, and the disturbance is roughly six foot by roughly three foot wide, and goes down at least a metre, then generally speaking, you're probably looking at a grave," Mr Hunter said.

After more than 14 years of feeding and watering guests, popular CBD tavern Lalla Rookh Bar & Eating House has announced that it will close at the end of 2026. “Fourteen years goes fast when you’re doing something you love,” says director Patrick Ryan. Tucked away in a basement space on Perth’s premier business terrace, Lalla Rookh was a favourite for workers in the CBD. “When we opened, we wanted to create a warm, unpretentious Italian restaurant and wine bar that the CBD could call its own. “What followed was incredible food, extraordinary wine, late nights, long lunches, celebrations, farewells, first dates, last drinks and everything in between.”

Advertisement

Or, in short, Lalla Rookh behaved just like any good pub: understandable, perhaps, when you consider that its basement address in Allendale Square has housed some famous CBD watering holes. (Hello Emporio, hello The Black Cat, hello The Foxy Lady.) Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up And while Lalla Rookh could still heave like any good public house worth its salt and vinegar chips – after-work drinks on a Friday were, pre-COVID, a heck of a time – it was also a quiet mover and shaker. Lalla Rookh’s wine store was highly regarded. Its dedicated 20-person wine store, for instance, was a prototype for the modern-day wine bar. Take a bow, Jeremy Prus: Lalla Rookh’s other director and a wine professional long regarded as the sommelier’s sommelier. (Prus, it’s worth mentioning, was also an early adopter of “natural wines”.)

If the occasion called for chips, pizza and other ballast to stave off the effects of all those beers and cocktails, they were there. But for those that were in the mood for dining, the kitchen could oblige with sharp modern Italian cooking from chefs such as Joel Valvasori-Pereza (Lulu La Delizia), Alexandra Haynes and Calum Mackechnie. Incumbent chef Michael Barnes is upholding Lalla’s reputation for approachable, quietly polished Italian flavours. But despite ticking the boxes for both quality and quantity – the space can hold up to 550 guests – Lalla Rookh, like many venues in the CBD, had been affected by Perth’s new corporate culture. Working from home hurt the lunch trade.

Changing attitudes to alcohol and cost of living pressures dampened consumer spending. While closure announcements often seem like they’ve come out of leftfield, Ryan and Prus say they’ve spent the last 18 months closely watching the market and crunching numbers, especially as they’ve approached the end of their lease.

There are two very distinct narratives emerging about artificial intelligence right now, and they’re both getting more extreme. You don’t need to be tuned into the debate to notice these two letters are appearing everywhere. AI is mentioned daily in the news, it’s brought up in work meetings, it appears in government policies and there’s barely a work conference where the topic if not discussed on and off stage. At one extreme are AI alarmists, who warn the technology is on a path to destruction. Marija Ercegovac What you think about the topic depends on which of the two extreme narratives you’re more likely to believe. At one end of the scale is the positive vision where the broad adoption of AI and robotics is on its way to creating a revolutionary new world. In this telling, goods and services will be dramatically cheaper, everyone will have access to high-quality healthcare and there will be little need to slave over much of the boring and time-consuming tasks that make up many people’s experience of work.

Advertisement

We do have one thing on our side right now, but not for much longer – and that is time. Elon Musk calls this “the age of abundance”, and Jeff Bezos predicted last week that a likely outcome of wide AI adoption would be the average person working just three days a week. Nvidia’s Jensen Huang told The New York Times last month that he thought it was a fallacy that AI would destroy jobs, and it will instead create even more jobs. Related Article Opinion

Holidays Why it’s time for you to ditch taking long annual holidays Tim Duggan Work columnist These grand visions of the future are driven primarily by the same tech oligarchs who are creating and selling this tech utopia. They want us to believe that everything will be better in their fantasies, with only pesky rights like privacy, truth and copyright needing to be sacrificed on the way there. At the other extreme end are AI alarmists, who conduct media tours warning us that the technology is on a path to destruction. It is self-improving at a pace that will soon be too powerful to control, they say, which could plausibly lead to cyberattacks, disinformation at scale, autonomous weapons or bioengineered pathogens that will threaten our very existence.

Advertisement

Many of these warnings on AI safety come from whistleblowing employees who have spent years working on the technology inside frontier labs, before deciding that they’ve now gone too far. One former Anthropic scientist, Evan Hubinger, resigned last month after giving a personal estimate that the risk of AI leading to the destruction of all humanity over the next decade is around 10 per cent. Related Article Opinion

Ask an expert From glowing feedback to undermining: Why has my boss turned on me? Jonathan Rivett Careers contributor These two extreme AI narratives – abundance or extinction – are both difficult to fully comprehend. Depending on which of them you lean towards will determine if you get excited every time an AI lab debuts a more powerful version of the technology, or if you wish they just downed their tools and stopped. But without any meaningful signs of regulation at their sources of these codes, primarily in the US and China, we’re all uncomfortably at their mercy. We do have one thing on our side right now, but not for much longer – and that is time. Despite all the recent advances, we are still at the stage of the technology when we can impact its outcome. It is still not too late for inbuilt safety checks across the leading frontier labs, government regulation, or even an agreed pause on the development to allow everyone to catch up. We need time to think about all the possible outcomes, formulate and debate legislation, agree on compromises and decide what kind of future we want.

Advertisement

That window of time is closing fast, but it’s still open for now. Is AI going to save us or destroy us? The answer depends on which of the two extreme ends of the narrative you’re more likely to believe, but the vast and growing valley between them is too wide to ignore. Breaking NationalVictoriaVictorian election ‘Oh no’: $285m COVID cover-up exposed by whistleblowers Patrick Hatch Updated October 15, 2026 — 2:39pm ,first published 11:27am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Two senior bureaucrats tried to cover up a suspected $285 million bungle that saw COVID-19 payments made to ineligible businesses by withholding information from their boss and government ministers. A report by the Independent Broad-based Anti-corruption Commission (IBAC) released on Thursday revealed that “false and misleading information” was provided to then-minister Martin Pakula in November 2021 in a bid to hide the fact that almost one quarter of the state’s program grants had been paid in error. Bourke Street was virtually empty during a Melbourne lockdown in 2020. Jason South The corruption watchdog’s investigation focused on the $4.5 billion Business Costs Assistance Program, which delivered up to $97,200 to businesses affected by state’s pandemic lockdown measures in 2020 and 2021. IBAC found that in November 2021, public servants in the Department of Jobs, Precincts and Regions identified that more than 9000 ineligible businesses had claimed an estimated $285 million worth of grants by backdating their GST registrations.

Advertisement

GST registration was a key criterion for eligibility, but the department did not appreciate the risk that businesses could legally backdate this by up to four years. Related Article Analysis

IBAC Victoria’s anti-corruption watchdog finally has teeth. These are its new powers At the time of assessing businesses, the department checked eligibility using a live database that updated as people backdated their GST registrations, rather than a static dataset that would have reflected eligibility at the time each grant was announced, IBAC found. Though the department initially estimated the total amount to be $285 million, the commission’s own analysis found that approximately $257 million was paid to ineligible businesses, with $108 million going to businesses that reported no activity in the six months leading up to the pandemic. To date, recipients who incorrectly received the grants have repaid about $8 million to the state government. Another $5 million is being returned through repayment plans, IBAC said.

Advertisement

The report says the department’s acting director of COVID-19 grants policy exclaimed “oh no” upon realising that almost one-fifth of the program’s funds had gone to ineligible applicants, and later remarked that it was “astonishing to realise how many snuck through”. In November 2021, a figure for “backdated GST registration … paid in error” losses was included in a draft Standing Directions report intended for the department’s secretary, Simon Phemister, and Pakula, then the minister for industry support and recovery. The investigation probed corrupt conduct by senior officials in the Department of Jobs, Precincts and Regions. The initial figure was listed as $8.92 million, but was revised to $251.9 million following further analysis by the department’s Integrity Services Unit. However, on November 30, 2021, the item was deleted from the report entirely at the request of a deputy secretary, the report says.

Advertisement

The deputy secretary told IBAC that the deletion followed “discussion and a decision that was reached above me”, noting that the department’s associate secretary was the most immediate person involved in those discussions. Editor's pick Opinion

Victorian election Forget political dust-ups – some of parliament’s best work never makes the front page Chip Le Grand State political editor The associate secretary told IBAC they did not draft or amend the report, or tell anyone to amend it. At the time, they believed the analysis leading to the overpayment figure was flawed, they said. A text message provided to IBAC showed the associate secretary telling the deputy secretary on December 3, 2025, that “I don’t think that problem re GST backdating overpayments is a problem. Phew”. However, IBAC said the associate secretary should have reported the analysis to the secretary, even if he disagreed with it.

Advertisement

IBAC said that “misleading information was subsequently created and disseminated over an extended period of time” as part of the cover-up, including to now-premier Ben Carroll in 2022 after he replaced Pakula as the relevant minister. The associate secretary also withheld key information from the Victorian Ombudsman, IBAC found. IBAC Commissioner Victoria Elliott said the investigation, named Operation Harmonia, uncovered behaviour contrary to the Victorian Public Sector code of conduct and “a clear failure to act in line with the high integrity standards expected of Victoria’s public officers”. Former minister for jobs, Martin Pakula, at a COVID-related press conference in 2021. Robert Cianflone/Getty Images “While officers within the department spoke up, their leaders failed to act, meaning the government was left uninformed and unable to move quickly to address this suspected significant loss of public funds,” he said.

Advertisement

Elliott applauded whistleblowers from within the Victorian public service who alerted IBAC to the cover-up and triggered its investigation. “Your bravery is critical in ensuring this conduct is not only exposed but that Victoria’s public sector can take these findings and apply the learnings to their own organisations,” he said. IBAC said it believed Phemister, the secretary, was not informed about the suspected loss, and that he was therefore unable to inform the minister about it. Pakula also told IBAC he was never informed of the issue. The report does not name the deputy secretary or associate secretary involved. title: Lung cancer rates in non-smokers like Pope Leo are rising. How can you catch it early?
