LifestyleHealth & wellnessLung cancer Lung cancer rates in non-smokers like Pope Leo are rising. How can you catch it early? Lauren Ironmonger Updated October 15, 2026 — 2:08pm ,first published 11:06am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Pope Leo XIV has announced he underwent surgery for lung cancer, after doctors detected a small growth on his lung during a routine health check. The Vatican said the Pope had lung adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer. Leo, 71, is a non-smoker. In Australia, lung cancer is the leading cause of death from cancer, killing more men and women annually than breast and prostate cancer combined, and is the fifth most diagnosed cancer. Despite this, detection rates remain low. Why? And what can you do to catch it early? Pope Leo is recovering from surgery for lung cancer. AP Photo/Andrew Medichini

Advertisement

What causes lung cancer? Globally, cases of lung cancer are increasing, particularly among young women who never smoked, according to research published by The World Health Organisation last year. The link between smoking and lung cancer is well-established, with co-ordinated public health campaigns over the past few decades helping rates of smoking drop significantly. This year, Australian researchers published a review with the strongest evidence yet that vaping is likely to cause lung and oral cancer. But Fraser Brims, deputy director of the Institute for Respiratory Health and professor at Curtin University, says environmental factors – like air pollution and radon, a natural gas – occupational exposure to dust, asbestos and silica, and genetics and family history can all contribute.

Advertisement

“One of the really important messages is that anybody with lungs can get lung cancer, and it’s certainly not just about smoking,” he says. Editor's pick Science The ‘unworthy’ cancer with a terrible survival rate and the program seeking to change it Evidence that exposure to incense or candle smoke causes cancer – despite information commonly circulated online – is inconclusive and there is no known risk, says Brims. Nor is risk merely shaped by individual lifestyle choices. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples disproportionately bear the burden of the disease in terms of diagnosis and mortality, alongside those living in regional and rural areas and from lower socioeconomic backgrounds.

Advertisement

Mark Brooke, Lung Foundation chief executive, says while most lung cancers have no symptoms in the early stages, the four most common signs are coughing up blood, persistent coughing, fatigue and weight loss. Lung cancer screening is Australia’s only risk-based screening program, unlike the bowel and breast cancer programs, which are age-based. Monique Westermann The stigma Despite plummeting smoking rates in countries like Australia, and rising lung cancer among non-smokers, the disease still carries stigma. “Australia is one of the worst in terms of this assumption and judging people against that. In no other type of cancer do we judge by a risk factor,” says Brims.

Advertisement

In Australia, 28 per cent of people admit they have less sympathy for someone with lung cancer compared with other forms of cancer, while one-third are unable to name one symptom. Lingering stigma, Brooke says, influences investment and donations. Compared to breast cancer, which has higher survivorship rates, lung cancer research receives around 30 per cent less funding. Loading How can you catch lung cancer early? Oncologists said Leo’s prognosis was “excellent” even before the operation due to early detection, according to the Associated Press.

Advertisement

Advertisement

Brooke says there is no evidence for making it a population-based screening program. “We have to weigh up the economic benefit versus the risks of having our population exposed to a CT scan on a frequent basis,” he says, adding non-specific screening also risks returning false positives, exposing individuals to invasive and potentially harmful medical interventions. Lung nodules – small growths found in lung tissue – can be found in up to half of people screened, but most are not related to cancer, says Brims. “It’s for us and medical teams to work out which ones we need to be most concerned about … the screening program’s process has so far proven very effective,” he says, adding they are working to identify and effectively target population groups most at risk. The Lung Foundation is calling on the government to increase eligibility to individuals aged 50 to 75 with a direct family history and those at risk of occupational exposure, alongside greater government research funding and more support for those diagnosed and their carers.

Advertisement

If you are concerned about your lung cancer risk or exhibit any “red flag” symptoms, like a lingering cough, Brooke urges individuals to “talk to your GP, explore your options for a CT scan and don’t delay”. The intercept included a higher-grade three-metre core going an eye-catching 7.75g/t gold. Impressively, the company says all 14 holes assayed at its Dulcie Central target have now intersected gold mineralisation, bolstering its interpretation of a continuous gold system. Zenith Minerals’ drilling at its Consolidated Dulcie Gold Project in Western Australia. The results come from a recently completed 34-hole reverse circulation drilling campaign across the broader project, with assays for 15 more holes now in hand. Zenith’s program is designed to test the roughly 600m strike gap between its existing Dulcie North and more southerly Dulcie deposits. Other results from the Dulcie Central corridor include a shallow, 10-metre intercept at 0.84g/t gold from just 48m, with another hole producing a three-metre strike running 1.59g/t gold from a similar depth. A third hole returned 2m at 1.57g/t gold from 97m and 3m grading 1.14g/t gold from 134m, hinting at the prospect of gold continuity at depth.

Further south again, at Dulcie South, a one-metre intercept came in at 3.86g/t gold from 128m. The Consolidated Dulcie project already hosts a significant JORC-compliant inferred mineral resource of 21.3 million tonnes grading 1g/t gold for 675,000 ounces across a 6-kilometre mineralised corridor. The grounds sit within the revered Southern Cross–Forrestania gold belt and benefit from granted mining leases and proximity to regional processing infrastructure at Marvel Loch and Edna May, placing it in prime real estate. Zenith Minerals managing director Andrew Smith said: “Every Dulcie Central hole assayed so far has intersected gold, with one hole returning the strongest intersection of the programme to date. These results continue to support the interpretation that gold mineralisation extends across the approximately 600-metre gap between Dulcie North and Dulcie.” While the company’s current program is focused on growing the resource, historical hits at the broader project have delivered some stunners such as 32m at 9.4g/t gold and 3m at an eye-watering 70g/t gold, highlighting the system’s high-grade pedigree.

Elsewhere, Zenith has a foothold on the promising Red Mountain gold project in Queensland, where previous drilling included a whopping 139.7m at 1.05g/t gold from 225m, which featured a richer 2-metre core assaying 21.03g/t gold within a broader 14.2m section grading 4.62g/t gold. Drilling has since traced gold mineralisation beyond 700m vertical depth, reinforcing the continuity of a broad intrusion-related gold system. The company also holds a 25 per cent free-carried interest at the emerging Earaheedy zinc project north-east of Wiluna in WA, alongside an indirect 26 per cent stake in the historic Cowarra gold project south of Canberra in New South Wales. Rounding out the portfolio, its Split Rocks lithium project in WA showcases an inferred JORC resource of 11.9Mt grading 0.72 per cent lithium oxide. With assays for 24 of the 34 holes back from the lab, attention is likely to turn to the final 10 holes, also all drilled within the promising 600-metre Dulcie Central corridor. Iron Bear’s namesake project sits in Labrador, Canada, one of the country’s premier iron ore districts. After a period of collaboration that saw its partner Vale sink US$18 million (A$25.8 million) into de-risking the colossal project in eastern Canada, the Brazilian behemoth has signalled its intent to bow out. Its departure leaves Iron Bear holding 100 per cent of a project with a recently completed prefeasibility study (PFS) valuing it at a staggering US$9 billion (A$12.8B) in net present value (NPV) - and that’s just on its conservative scenario. Yet the market has not exactly rewarded Iron Bear for its newfound freedom. Since Vale’s decision, Iron Bear’s valuation has been cut almost in half, suggesting investors have viewed the loss of the major partner as a doomsday event for future financing.

Advertisement

However, the market’s reaction appears to have overshadowed the enormous scale of Iron Bear’s multi-generational resource, its premium iron ore pellet product and the strategic importance of North American iron ore supply for cleaner steel production. For Vale, the decision, while surprising given the project’s immense value, fits with its broader shift towards investment opportunities closer to home. The iron ore giant has increasingly turned its attention to expanding its South American copper operations - pulling from the BHP playbook - and future local rare earth initiatives. Simultaneously, the company remains hamstrung by an enormous financial liability stemming from its 2010s tailings dam disasters. With billions tied up in remediation, compensation and dam decommissioning back home, a US$5 billion (A$7.15 billion) development some 9000 kilometres away has become a difficult proposition for an increasingly Brazilian-owned organisation, with lofty expectations of domestic reinvestment. Vale’s growing appetite for copper and its renewed focus on South American investments may have inadvertently dealt Iron Bear a winning hand. With full ownership restored, the junior is now free to pursue offtake agreements, streaming deals, financing or strategic partnership opportunities, all on its own terms. In mining, you rarely get someone else to do the heavy lifting before handing you back the whole prize. By any measure, the Iron Bear project is a monster. It hosts a JORC resource of 13.6 billion tonnes grading 30 per cent iron and containing more of the steelmaking metal than Rio Tinto’s fabled “Pilbara Killer” Simandou, in Guinea, West Africa. The resource at Iron Bear is so vast that its initial 44-year mine plan touches less than a quarter of the known deposit.

Advertisement

The company says the deposit is a typical Labrador Trough taconite, a hard, iron-rich rock deposit that has underpinned mining in the region for over half a century. The district already hosts successful producers, including ASX-listed Champion Iron, whose Bloom Lake operation is a proven economic model for turning this type of ore into high-value products. However, Iron Bear would seem to be playing in a different league. Its maiden probable ore reserve of 3.3 billion tonnes is roughly five times bigger than Bloom Lake’s entire reserve base and its total resource is an order of magnitude greater. It was this sheer, multi-generational scale that attracted Vale to Canada, leading to a binding agreement that would have seen the major fund up to US$138 million in development costs to earn a whopping 75 per cent stake. For a junior developer, the deal was transformative. It wasn’t just the funding; it was the third-party validation and access to Vale’s immense technical expertise. Over the subsequent period, Vale’s top engineers worked alongside the Iron Bear crew, deploying serious capital to advance the project towards a PFS. That study, delivered by the highly respected Hatch engineering group, landed with a thud, confirming the project’s world-class potential. The PFS outlined a 44-year operation at 23 million tonnes of iron ore annually. It projected a post-tax NPV of US$9 billion and an internal rate of return of 15.2 per cent - more than suitable for major players looking for multi-decade production.

Advertisement

Perhaps even more importantly, the whole operation is slated to run entirely on extremely cheap, renewable hydropower. And with the Canadian government actively encouraging new resource development while keeping emissions low for its citizens, a high-purity critical minerals project like Iron Bear could be just the ticket. Recent federal legislation has reopened accelerated project approvals for “projects of national significance” - a status that Iron Bear has already applied for. If successful, this could significantly shorten the permitting timeline in Labrador and further de-risk the project for investment. Adding to the robust economics is the project’s prime location for infrastructure. It sits less than 35 kilometres from an open-access, heavy-haul railway that connects directly to the deep-water port of Sept-Iles, North America’s biggest mineral port. Iron Bear’s premium Direct Reduction pellets, crucial feed for DR steel production, a clean technology to produce steel using natural gas or hydrogen instead of coal. Equally compelling, the study confirmed the project’s ability to produce a premium product tailor-made for the future of steelmaking.

Advertisement

Iron Bear’s pilot plant testwork has confirmed the taconite ore can be upgraded to a 71 per cent iron concentrate suitable for the increasingly sought after Direct Reduction (DR) steelmaking. The pathway to so-called “green steel” is achievable only through DR plants that can be powered by natural gas or, ultimately, green hydrogen, slashing carbon emissions compared to traditional coal-fired blast furnaces. The premium DR grade product commands a hefty premium over benchmark 62 per cent iron ore fines, with Iron Bear tipping demand to surge 50 per cent over the next decade as steelmakers chase cleaner production. With premium DR-grade pellets fetching up to US$225 a tonne in the spot market, the right offtake deal could lock in future sales while delivering valuable upfront financing to help bankroll the mine’s development. Armed with A$15.3 million in cash, a completed PFS and full ownership of its colossal Canadian asset, Iron Bear now resembles a newly single eligible bachelor - suddenly free to court top-tier offtakers on its own terms. Losing a major partner is rarely cause for celebration, yet Iron Bear has emerged with a project scrutinised and de-risked alongside one of the world’s biggest iron ore producers, with the entire prize back in its own hands. The company’s challenge now is to turn a significant head start into a development deal worthy of a once-in-a-generation resource and its US$9 billion NPV, potentially cementing its place among North America’s most strategic iron ore assets. title: Why I have an issue with the Nick Blakey trade to North Melbourne
text:

SportAFLAFL 2026 Opinion Why I have an issue with the Nick Blakey trade to North Melbourne Peter Ryan Sports reporter October 15, 2026 — 1:08pm

October 15, 2026 — 1:08pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Nick Blakey is an excellent footballer, an All-Australian defender in the prime of his career with speed and a lethal left foot. North Melbourne officials were excited to land him in this trade period for that reason, but it was no ordinary trade that sent him from Sydney to the Kangaroos. Nick Blakey dons the North Melbourne guernsey. Nathan John, North Melbourne FC That’s because Blakey remains one of four AFL players still subject to a Victoria Police investigation into allegations of sexual assault at the Pullman hotel, where the Swans were staying after beating Essendon at the MCG in round 23. The five players who were suspended by Sydney for breaching behavioural standards, including Blakey, have consistently denied any wrongdoing. None have been charged.

Advertisement

But it remains a challenging situation, particularly for the women who made the allegations. Because, less than two months later and with that police investigation unresolved, a club board decided to offer one of the players involved a spot in their team, and for a salary close to $12 million over eight years. In what world does that happen? We have the answer: in the AFL, where a club exists to win and any concerns about behaviour can be addressed with an apology and a promise to do better.

Advertisement

Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 From Pullman to pulling power: How Nick Blakey profited from scandal and the AFL’s strange economy That is all Blakey can really do. His dissatisfaction with the Swans shows he doesn’t believe his involvement in whatever may have happened at the Pullman has been fairly reflected in Sydney’s decisions. My discomfort with the trade is not directed towards him. My issue is that the club’s decision and the AFL’s willingness to wave it through makes all the virtue-signalling words the industry uses ring hollow. The league creates an impression that it is a leader on social issues, which carries an assumed yet laughable mortgage on defining what makes someone “a good person”. CEO Andrew Dillon wrote in the days after the Pullman incident: “Our first question should not be what this means for a football club. It should be whether our actions match the standards we stand for and the community expects of us. “As a sport, and as an industry, we are clear about the standards we expect and the values we stand for and the need to uphold them.

Advertisement

“Being clear about our standards also means being prepared to act when those standards are not met.” Sydney acted. They took a strong stand to show they stood for more than just winning, and it cost them. AFL chief executive Andrew Dillon made a strong statement about the standards players and officials should meet in the days following the Pullman incident. Eddie Jim North Melbourne certainly acted. They now have Blakey on more money than anyone else at the club. The Roos showed it was one club taking a stand, rather than the industry, by seizing on the opportunity Sydney’s approach presented them.

Advertisement

Related Article AFL 2026 Wife of top AFL executive voices concern over Nick Blakey trade deal The AFL will say it can’t dictate to the clubs what they do during trade period, particularly during an active police investigation. But every decision reflects on the league, and the size of the deal is incongruous with those words from a month ago. The AFL waving the trade through implies, whether true or not, that the league knows something we don’t. Surely a club wouldn’t sign a player to such a long-term deal and give away such draft capital if it wasn’t confident he would line up the next season. Actions speak louder than words and the trade showed in stark reality that the defining feature of the game at the highest level is how well you play it and the rest can be, to use a football cliche, worked through. That’s fine and not unexpected, but spare us the bullshit. The right many in the game assume – to lead on social issues – is disappearing before our eyes. That’s unfortunate because their power to influence is unquestionable.

Advertisement

That’s why this trade is challenging for those who love footy, as the decisions the players made that night – regardless of whether anything criminal may have occurred – were out of step with the expectations that clubs and supporters have of players. Seeing one of them rewarded financially so soon after just felt wrong. North Melbourne’s offer is challenging for volunteers working their guts out to maintain great community football clubs with inclusive environments for no reward except in giving people a safe place to gather on the weekend. It will be challenging to people within the North Melbourne Football Club and at other AFL clubs who sell a vision that tries to create a purpose beyond merely winning. North Melbourne players and staff members are now representatives of the decision to bring Blakey on board – whether they like it or not.

Advertisement

They will be muted in what they can say because anyone who objects is in for a fight. The machine operates at full tilt to support those who entertain rather than complain. The Kangaroos decided to communicate the reasons behind their decision to staff and their premiership-winning AFLW team. The forum wasn’t an opportunity to approve or object to those reasons, as such. It was so that everyone understood the club’s reasoning, while giving a chance for questions about how to respond to stakeholders when queries about the decision inevitably arise. Loading But even if it had been a forum for debate, would anyone who objected have been perceived as difficult? The Roos have built a strong culture under impressive leadership from the president Sonja Hood and CEO Jen Watt. And they are a football club with the primary aim of winning games. That’s understood and has been reinforced time and time again across all the clubs.

Advertisement

Perhaps it’s the pretence that it means something more that irks the most. The salient question for North to answer is this: what gives them the confidence they can absorb Blakey into their program and maintain a strong culture when questions abound about the players’ behaviour at the Pullman? AFL players (from left) Chad Warner, James Jordon, Isaac Heeney and Nick Blakey are still subject to a police investigation. The Age Having entered into such a big contract, will they pull up behaviour if performance is strong? They can argue they showed that capacity when they cut Tarryn Thomas for “inappropriate treatment of women” in 2024.

Advertisement

Meanwhile, the league will argue it can’t do anything of substance until the police investigation concludes. Currently, it seems the outcome of that police investigation will determine the AFL and industry’s standards. Because the hand-wringing that followed the Pullman incident, and the concern for the women making the complaints that were so frequently expressed before footy issues were discussed back in August, are no longer part of the script. I am not in a position to lecture and won’t go down that path. But now that we understand through research, such as what’s laid out on Our Watch’s website, that “gender inequality sets the underlying context for violence against women”, we should all be prepared to do better.

title: For years, it led nowhere. Now North Korea is opening it
text:
In brief A new bridge between North Korea and China has been opened, 12 years after it was completed.

The move is expected to strengthen trade between the two countries.

A new bridge linking China and North Korea opened on Thursday after more than a decade of delay in the latest sign of closer ties between the two countries.

The four-lane, 3km New Yalu River Bridge will connect the north-eastern Chinese city of Dandong to the North Korean city of Sinuiju.

Trucks bearing the North Korean and Chinese flags began passing in both directions over the bridge in the late morning, reporters for the Agence France-Presse news agency at the scene said.

The bridge was first expected to open in 2014 after China apparently completed construction of access roads, customs facilities and other related infrastructure on its side. But the date passed with no sign of an opening and without North Korea doing corresponding works on its side.

At that time, it prompted an unusually sharp report in the Global Times, a newspaper affiliated with the Chinese Communist Party, which quoted Dandong residents expressing frustration over delays in what they had hoped would be an economic boon for their border city.

A lack of substantial work on the North Korean side prompted speculation that North Korea was wary of an increase in economic dependence or was unhappy with China voting for United Nations resolutions toughening international sanctions on the North over its nuclear program. Some observers said North Korea and China also differed over the location of the bridge.

Bridge expected to bolster trade links

A Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson said on Wednesday the new bridge will further promote economic, trade and "people-to-people exchanges".

"China and the DPRK [Democratic People's Republic of Korea] are friendly neighbours linked by rivers and mountains," Mao Ning said. She added the bridge is an important "project for connectivity" between the two countries.

The new link is expected to lessen the burden on an existing yet aging bridge on the Dandong-Sinuiju route, which handles more than 70 per cent of official trade between the two countries. The old bridge built in 1937 carries a railway line as well as cars and trucks, but vehicle traffic can move only one way at a time.

The South Korean government said last year there were at least 17 active road and rail links across the porous North Korea-China border, which stretches more than 1,400km.

The new bridge's opening will likely boost bilateral trade and enhance logistical efficiency gradually. But in the short term, trade won't likely result in a sharp increase in Chinese exports to North Korea as Beijing would take Pyongyang's interests into consideration to some extent, according to a recent report by Gyubeom Kim, an expert at Seoul's state-run Institute for National Security Strategy.

North Korea's export of processed goods, food products, cosmetics and alcoholic beverages to China could increase, Kim said.

Relations with Russia and China

The bridge's opening comes about a month after North Korea and Russia opened a 1km road bridge over the Tumen River as part of their efforts to cement relations.

Experts say Chinese officials likely felt uneasy about the opening of the North Korea-Russia bridge, which the Russian government said would allow daily passage of up to 300 vehicles through a newly built border crossing point.

The North Korea-China bridge is much bigger and likely capable of carrying round-the-clock, two-way traffic including containers and heavy cargo trucks, according to Jeong Eun-i, an analyst from South Korea's Institute for National Unification.

China has long been North Korea's biggest trading partner and economic pipeline. But in past years, North Korean leader Kim Jong-un has prioritised Moscow, sending thousands of troops and conventional weapons to support Russian President Vladimir Putin's war in Ukraine, apparently in exchange for military and economic assistance.

Kim has recently drawn closer to China with the apparent intent to improve the economy and build a front against the United States. China, for its part, wants to restore its unique influence over North Korea. Last year, about 98 per cent of North Korea's external trade was with China.

The bridge's opening has been anticipated since Chinese President Xi Jinping travelled to Pyongyang in June for a meeting with Kim. During their summit, Xi expressed Beijing's willingness to expand bilateral cooperation in trade, agriculture, construction and technology, while Kim described ties with China as a top strategic priority.

title: The $2.9 trillion corner of Australia's economy at the centre of a tax war
text:
Key Points Small business groups warn 350,000 family firms face higher taxes or costly restructures.

Coalition vows to repeal changes as compliance costs top $1 billion.

A multi-billion-dollar gap and a reignited political divide has opened up between small businesses and the government over a new policy taxing trillion-dollar trust schemes.

The government plans to close a tax advantage many workers can't access by imposing a minimum 30 per cent tax on the net income of 840,000 trusts that allow wealthy investors and family businesses to spread income across their family or obscure asset ownership in bankruptcy and family-court proceedings. Australian trusts have combined assets of $2.9 trillion with annual income of $600 billion.

The changes are projected to raise $4.47 billion in 2029/30 after they begin on 1 July 2028. Treasury data shows trusts are overwhelmingly used by Australia's top 10 per cent of income earners who receive about two-thirds of distributions, while the bottom 10 per cent receive one per cent.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers said the reforms affect fewer than 10 per cent of small businesses.

"Small businesses and others using discretionary trusts can access rollover relief from 1 July 2027 if they want to restructure, or can make an election for tax purposes to be exempt from the minimum tax, for as long as they continue to make distributions to pre-nominated beneficiaries in line with an upfront nomination," Chalmers said on Wednesday.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Senior economist at the left-wing thinktank the Australia Institute, David Richardson, told SBS News the changes plug a tax-dodging loophole used by wealthy people to spread income across their family or obscure asset ownership in bankruptcy and family-court proceedings.

"The ambiguity of who owns what in the trust means they become a vehicle for putting assets away, where it's very hard for bankruptcy proceedings to access them," Richardson said. "It's hard for the Family Court to know what's going on. So, generally, family trusts, even when they're taxed at 30 per cent, will still be useful for somebody on very high incomes, where the marginal tax rate is 47 cents."

That small businesses, and others are unhappy with the change, "shows you that they're presently doing well out of a trust structure", he said.

"They wouldn't be complaining unless they were genuinely avoiding what they would have to pay as either an individual sole trader or as the principal of some sort of corporate structure."

Australian Council of Social Service CEO Dr Cassandra Goldie said the reforms restore some "basic economic fairness".

"It is not fair that someone earning $200,000 or more, who would usually pay 47 per cent tax on extra income, can bring that rate down to 30 per cent or less by passing income through a discretionary trust to their adult children or a private company, while an average worker pays tax at a rate of 30 per cent of the next dollar earned," Goldie said.

Why are small businesses unhappy?

The Council of Small Business Organisations Australia CEO Skye Cappuccio said after months of consultation "fundamental problems" remain, forcing 350,000 family and small businesses structured this way to choose between "a substantial tax increase", or restructuring costs in the thousands of dollars for professional fees, duties and administration.

Credit: Australia Institute

"These are not genuine choices. They are bad options that will make operating a small family business harder and more expensive," Cappuccio said.

"These are small family businesses that have legitimately used trusts for decades to protect assets, manage succession and plan for the future," Cappuccio said.

"This policy targets a business structure rather than the conduct the government is concerned about. There are more targeted ways to address tax integrity without imposing unnecessary costs on genuine small businesses.

"Queensland and Western Australian enterprises will be hit hardest by the changes because stamp duty may apply if a business there restructures its assets."

What's the political divide and controversy?

The Coalition failed to stall the laws on Wednesday, but opposition leader Angus Taylor said the Coalition will go to the election with a "policy of axing the tax".

Opposition treasury spokesperson Tim Wilson said, "small and family businesses face a bill of up to $13.3 billion for the cost of valuations, advisers and stamp duty because our taxaholic treasurer broke his election promise and can’t kick his spending addiction".

"The treasurer has rewritten this tax again and again since budget night because he doesn’t understand his own policy or the damage it does. Every backdown is an admission it should never have been proposed in the first place," Wilson said.

Trusts excluded from the changes include deceased estates, disability, superannuation, charities, farms and fixed trusts.

READ MORE How the ATO found itself embroiled in a battle over credit cards that forced a rethink

The Housing Industry Association warned this is a new tax on tradies, and builders that diverts their attention from building the homes Australia desperately needs."

Greens leader David Shoebridge said on Wednesday there are too many concessions being made and will refer the bill to a Senate inquiry and that claims about restructuring costs should be supported by detailed modelling.

"We want to make sure that we don't, in passing this legislation, create that additional loophole," Shoebridge said. "This is about ensuring that there's a fair level playing field across business, but also across society, and that's our focus.

"If the Coalition is going to put a figure out like that ($13 billion), they need to back it up with numbers (and modelling)."

Will this really cost businesses $13 billion?

Treasury estimates the cost to businesses will be $141.5 million annually plus $940 million during an implementation phase.

But the Coalition and Wilson say the cost will be up to $13.3 billion based on a Wilson Asset Management estimate.

Wilson ran a successful campaign against changes to franking credits by coordinating with Wilson Asset Management in 2019.

But CPA Australia tax lead Jenny Wong told SBS News the Coalition’s figure includes stamp duty, and Treasury’s doesn’t. But there is no source or method listed as to how they arrived at their number.

"Our estimate is $2 billion to $2.8 billion, for advice alone (and) covers the cost of working out what to do across roughly 850,000 trusts, before anyone restructures or elects (beneficiaries)," Wong said. "The bill leaves 12 rules to be made later by the minister, up from 10, and ATO [Australian Taxation Office] guidance won’t come until after the law passes."

The government has given families a way to avoid restructuring, and "that deserves credit", she said.

"But for those who still have to restructure, nothing in this bill makes it cheaper. Stamp duty can be most of the bill, and the Commonwealth can’t waive it,” Wong said.

"We support dealing with inappropriate income splitting (done) simply, fairly and in proportion," Wong said. "On that test, there is still work to do."

Treasury's analysis estimates that restructuring a family business can cost between $9,536 and $23,436 and that restructuring could cost family businesses more than the tax itself.

title: 'Deeply disappointing': Australia joins allies in voicing concerns over Palestinian election delays
text:
Foreign Minister Penny Wong has issued a joint statement with her counterparts in Canada, France and the United Kingdom describing a delay to Palestinian elections as "deeply disappointing".

Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas postponed next month's legislative council and presidential elections to next year, after concerns that conditions in Gaza and the West Bank were not conducive to holding elections.

The foreign ministers called on the Palestinian Authority to reconsider its decision and to take the necessary steps to hold the elections without further delay.

"We acknowledge that significant challenges and impediments have affected the ability to conduct elections in a manner fully consistent with international standards and with the participation of all eligible Palestinians," they said.

"Credible elections are an important element of the commitment that President Abbas and the Palestinian Authority made to reform, including democratic renewal and accountable governance."

title: Russian facilities were attacked. Then came a viral theory
text:
Key Points Ukraine has launched strikes on three data centres used by Russian technology platform Yandex over the last week.

Several posts claiming a resulting decrease in Russian bot activity have been widely circulated.

A series of Ukrainian strikes on data centres in Russia had Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy claiming an additional win.

"When our strikes reached Yandex’s data centres, it suddenly became a little easier to breathe on many social media platforms," he told participants at the Warsaw Security Forum this week.

"There was less hate, less division, and fewer provocations. Because there were fewer bots."

Russia had previously targeted Ukrainian data centres and telecommunication infrastructure.

But as the latest round of strikes had users celebrating a drop in Russian misinformation, experts say the reality is more complicated.

A change in web traffic

In the past week, Ukraine has struck three of the five main data centres used by Russian technology company Yandex, often considered Russia's version of Google.

A widely shared graph of data from US tech firm Cloudflare showed a sharp drop-off for bot traffic shortly after one of the strikes.

A Polish political scientist shared a post linking the strikes to a sharp drop in activity supportive of Germany's far-right AfD party. He later deleted the X post after finding the graph was AI-generated, but it had already circulated widely. A similar graphic was also shared by a Czech member of the European Parliament on X.

The Ukrainian strikes damaged Yandex infrastructure, with a Kremlin spokesperson saying the provider was "currently facing difficulties".

Yandex is used for search, email, file storage, food delivery, ride-sharing, and more in Russia. Source: AAP / Kirill Kukhmar

Olivia Shen is the director of strategic technologies at the United States Studies Centre. She says while a drop in bot traffic from Yandex has been observed, there has been no definitive evidence that it resulted in an impact on dis- or misinformation.

"A company like Yandex has bots crawl on the internet all the time, but they do really basic things like indexing web pages and optimising its search engines, just as you would expect Google to do," she said.

"So, it's not really surprising that when the Yandex data centres are taken out of action, there's fewer Yandex bots sending out automated requests to websites.

"Not all bots are equal, and they don't all do the same thing."

What are bots?

The term bot is used to describe any automated process completed online. It's also, however, often used to describe the actions of malicious actors.

Dr Kateryna Kasianenko studies how online searching practices relate to real-world crises. She said Cloudflare uses a broad definition of bots.

"There is a chance that what we call social media bots on Russia's side would have been impacted by [the strikes]. But the extent of that is quite hard to evaluate at this stage," she said.

"It's been really interesting to see the attempts to actually evaluate whether or not there was indeed a drop in engagement or also the spread of problematic narratives on Russia's behalf and actors that Russia may support, like AfD, Donald Trump and others.

"The evidence so far is quite mixed."

Kasianenko says it has brought more attention to "the mechanics behind Russia's efforts to control [the] information space".

She says it's quite hard for a regular user to accurately identify whether something online was created by a person or a bot, especially when the interaction involves amplification, such as liking and reposting content.

"Russia does deploy a mixed approach where they have these very handcrafted, deliberate human messages, and they also use automation for things like amplification, retweeting and likes," she said.

"It's very hard to know whether those types of engagements were generated by a human or an automated account."

Shen says this is further complicated by a tendency to label difficult viewpoints as bots, rather than grappling with the complexity of differing beliefs held within Russia.

"I don't think just dismissing those views, those legitimately held views as mis- or disinformation, or as the behaviour of bots, is helpful in bridging those gaps between Russians and Ukrainians or Russians and the rest of the world," she said.

A perceived decline in pro-Russian views online could be explained by Russian citizens not being able to access the internet, instead of damage to bot networks.

Dr Olga Boichak, a senior lecturer in digital cultures at the University of Sydney, researches the weaponisation of digital technologies. She says we need more research to empirically prove whether a sizeable reduction in the amount of troll and bot messaging has occurred. Shen said this situation is "a perfect opportunity for a natural experiment to actually collect the data on that".

The physical dimension of misinformation

Boichak said these strikes have exposed a critical vulnerability: "physical infrastructure matters".

Mis- and disinformation are normally treated as activities happening online, but she said the breadth of potential forms it can take makes it difficult to contain.

"Not all of them involve spreading falsehoods. Sometimes it would be manufacturing a few competing versions of truth. Sometimes it would be circulating different rumours. Sometimes it will be circulating memes. Sometimes it would be bullying and harassment of the people who are activists or working in some space," she said.

"Our traditional containment methods sometimes fall short because they don't recognise something as an influence operation.

"I think that is a big lesson here that democracies need to consider various other ways, ways that are deeper in the infrastructural levels to contain these attempts and disinformation."

Data centres are becoming an increasingly acceptable military target, according to Shen.

"I think that's a bit concerning because this is digital infrastructure that takes down the internet for a lot of ordinary users, not just military operatives or people deliberately spreading influence campaigns," she said.

Boichak says Russia's regime of "digital authoritarianism" makes damage to physical infrastructure more severe, with much of the country reliant on Yandex, as a result of the ongoing blocking of Western platforms.

title: A second Eurovision contest is approaching. Here's how Australians can watch
text:
IN BRIEF: The first-ever Eurovision Asia will come to Australian screens in November.

Meanwhile, applications to represent Australia in Eurovision 2027 will open soon.

Australians will be treated to a second instalment of Eurovision this year, as the competition's first Asia series will broadcast from Bangkok in November.

On 14 November, 11 countries will take to the stage in Thailand's capital for the grand final of the first Eurovision Song Contest Asia.

Eurovision Asia's first competitors revealed

The contest will feature artists representing Bangladesh, Bhutan, Cambodia, Laos, Malaysia, Mongolia, Nepal, the Philippines, the Republic of Korea, Thailand, and Vietnam, and will be broadcast live on SBS.

Multi-hyphenate entertainer and global icon Courtney Act will steer the show, returning as SBS' Eurovision commentator.

More than 3.27 million Australians tuned in to Eurovision on SBS this year, where Courtney Act and special guest commentator Danny Estrin guided audiences through the spectacle of the world's biggest music entertainment event.

Eurovision Asia will be no exception, with Thai television personalities Woody Milintachinda, known for hosting the talk shows Woody Talk and Woody Kerd Ma Kui and model, actress, TV host and activist Cindy Bishop hosting the inaugural event.

A decade-long journey to the stage

The project has been in the making for a decade, with the original proposal for an Asia-Pacific iteration of the popular song contest driven by SBS.

Artists are invited to register their interest in representing Australia, and songwriters to submit an original song for consideration via the SBS Song Portal for Eurovision 2027.

Eligible songs must run for no longer than three minutes, include at least one Australian citizen in the songwriting team, and not have been released or publicly performed, in whole or in part, before 1 September.

Australia's 2027 entry will be selected through an internal SBS process, and submitting a song or registering interest through the portal does not guarantee selection.

title: Matildas thrash Haiti as World Cup preparations continue
text:
In brief The Matildas have defeated Haiti in an international friendly match.

Midfielder Leticia McKenna delivered a powerful performance, scoring two goals.

The Matildas bounced back from a defeat to Germany with a commanding 7-1 win over Haiti as they continue preparing for the FIFA Women's World Cup.

Matildas midfielder Leticia McKenna boosted her chances of selection for her first FIFA Women's World Cup after scoring twice.

Fresh off a humbling 4-2 defeat to powerhouse Germany, and without Arsenal star Steph Catley, Australia got their World Cup preparations back on track in Chambly, France on Wednesday.

McKenna was the spark, as she produced two classy first-half strikes before an own goal by Haiti defender Kethna Louis.

Goals to Caitlin Foord, Daniela Galic, Clare Wheeler and Holly McNamara completed the victory.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

The Nottingham Forest midfielder has now secured three goals in four national team appearances, adding a selection headache for coach Joe Montemurro.

When the Matildas mentor was asked if he thought his team was ready for next year's World Cup, he laughed and said "no".

"We need time ... It's probably more about selecting the squad because now we're starting to build a big roster of players, and I need more time to make a decision on who I can bring," Montemurro said.

"It was a good window for us. We played against Germany ... We felt that we were not far, and we know the areas where we need to fix."

READ MORE Two goals but no win for Matildas in Germany friendly

Along with McKenna, the Australians midfield produced a masterclass as Alana Murphy dispatched a crafty pass to set up Galic while Wheeler had an assist and goal.

"I was a spectator in 2023, and I loved watching the group. It only made me hungrier to want to be a part of it," McKenna said.

"So to be in a position to potentially be selected is amazing."

Matildas dominate in second half

Questions had loomed over captain and star striker Sam Kerr's fitness after she complained of ankle soreness following the German clash, but she was also influential, playing a big role in two of the goals.

The rousing victory helped the Matildas firmly keep their No.15 world ranking, which currently puts them in pot two out of four for the World Cup draw, meaning a mathematically better chance for a more favourable draw.

It wasn't a smooth-sailing win for Montemurro's players though, as their first-half defence looked timid when their Caribbean opponents employed their counterattack, but they utterly dominated the second half as Haiti's wheels fell off.

It took just 80 seconds for the Matildas to draw first blood when Wheeler cut the ball back to McKenna, who produced a sublime one-touch strike into the roof of the net.

But moments later, Haitian midfield star Melchie Dumornay tucked the ball into the bottom right corner to equalise.

On the stroke of halftime, McKenna re-established the Australians' lead when she pounced on a loose ball in the box and buried it in the bottom left corner.

In the 53rd minute, Foord poked the ball to Kerr, who steered it goalwards and found the foot of Louis.

The sparkling Foord-Kerr combination wreaked havoc again when the Arsenal winger scored before substitute Galic found her first international goal.

Wheeler added her name to the scoresheet when her cross bound for Foord snuck into the bottom left corner before McNamara iced the game.

title: 'Voice for peace': Albanese sends Pope Leo well wishes after cancer diagnosis
text:
In brief Pope Leo had a lower lobe of his lung removed in a surgery and has been diagnosed with lung cancer.

The surgery was successful with no complications, according to the Vatican.

Pope Leo had a lower lobe of his right lung removed during surgery and was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma, a common form of lung cancer, the Vatican said in a medical bulletin.

Leo, 71, was admitted to Rome's Gemelli hospital on Tuesday for surgery to remove a growth on his lung that doctors found in a recent health checkup.

Tuesday's surgery lasted about 90 minutes and was successful with no complications, the Vatican said. The pope has woken up normally and is resting in his hospital room.

The Vatican said previously that the pope was expected to spend a week in hospital recovering.

Asked if there was any sign that the cancer had spread further, a Vatican source said further tests were being carried out.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said his "thoughts and prayers" were with the pontiff, calling him "a voice for peace, humanity and reason in our modern world".

"Pope Leo XIV is a source of inspiration to Catholics right around the world — and here in Australia," he said in a post on X.

"We hope and pray for a quick recovery."

The surgery marked the pope's first hospitalisation since he became head of the Catholic Church on 8 May 2025. Chicago-born Leo, the first US pope, is sporty and was believed to generally be in good health.

In a surprise announcement following Angelus prayers on Sunday, Leo told crowds in Rome's St Peter's Square that doctors had discovered the nodule "at a very early stage" during medical checks.

"The doctors believe it would be right to intervene," he said.

The Vatican has historically been very secretive about the health of popes, but began to be more transparent during the illness of Leo's predecessor Francis, an Argentine who freely discussed his ailments.

Ahead of the surgery, the Vatican said the pope's recovery time was expected to be about a week. His audiences have been cancelled until 20 October.

He is scheduled to travel to South America from 6 to 17 November to visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru.

It's not immediately clear what will happen if the pope requires a longer treatment or recovery.

Under church law, a figure known as the Cardinal Camerlengo — or chamberlain — takes over administrative duties if the pope dies, but pontiffs do not have a deputy to replace them if they become incapacitated.

title: She was once engaged to Donald Trump Jr. Now the White House wants her to resign
text:
In brief The Trump administration has asked Kimberly Guilfoyle to resign as US ambassador to Greece.

The former Fox News host has been embroiled in corruption allegations. She denies wrongdoing.

United States President Donald Trump's administration has asked his ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle to resign, the White House said, amid allegations that she sought money from a Trump supporter and accepted lavish hospitality from wealthy Greek businessmen.

"We have asked Ambassador Guilfoyle to resign," Trump's new press secretary Katie Zacharia told reporters at her first White House briefing.

The announcement came a day after Trump acknowledged that he was considering dismissing Guilfoyle, a former Fox News host and ex-fiancée of his eldest son, Donald Trump Jr.

"She was doing a good job, but we didn't like what we were reading," Trump told reporters after the announcement, adding that he had not spoken to her, but that "she will not be there".

In a statement on X, Guilfoyle appeared to confirm she would leave her post. She rejected the allegations against her and defended her record as ambassador, highlighting efforts to boost US energy exports and strengthen security ties with Greece.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"These allegations are false, and I intend to vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity," she wrote.

Guilfoyle thanked Trump and secretary of state Marco Rubio, pledging her continued loyalty to the president.

"While my time as Ambassador may be coming to an end, my commitment to President Trump, the America First movement, and the country I love will never end," she wrote.

Guilfoyle has faced mounting scrutiny following a series of reports by The Wall Street Journal about her financial dealings and relationships with wealthy businessmen.

The newspaper reported that she asked Eric Deters, an influential Trump supporter, to pay off $100,000 in personal credit card debt shortly before her Senate confirmation hearing in July 2025.

Guilfoyle, a former Fox News host, served as an adviser to Donald Trump's 2024 presidential campaign. Source: Getty / Bloomberg

"Honey please I need you to get this done for me today," she wrote to Deters in a message accompanied by instructions for paying her credit card company, according to the Journal, which published screenshots of the exchanges.

Deters refused to make the payment, telling the newspaper that doing so would have cost him his marriage.

Guilfoyle's lawyer has disputed the authenticity of the messages and denied wrongdoing.

Who is Kimberly Guilfoyle?

Guilfoyle, a prominent figure in Trump's Make America Great Again movement, was appointed ambassador after her relationship to Donald Trump Jr. ended quietly in 2024. They got engaged in 2020.

She played a prominent role in her father-in-law's political circles, including as an adviser to his 2024 presidential campaign.

A former prosecutor, she was married to California's Democratic governor Gavin Newsom between 2001 and 2005, before going on to work at Fox News.

She stayed in Trump's orbit following her split from his son, with the president announcing in December 2024 that he would nominate her to serve as ambassador to Greece.

She was confirmed by the Senate in September last year and sworn in the following month.

Ethics allegations

The Journal also reported that Guilfoyle boasted of luxury trips and hotel stays funded by wealthy Greek businessmen, citing hundreds of messages, emails and other records, including recorded conversations.

She travelled to the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, aboard a private jet with Alexandros Exarchou, chief executive of Greek construction company Aktor Group, according to the newspaper.

Guilfoyle also spent Christmas at the exclusive Swiss ski resort of Gstaad with Greek shipping magnate Nikolas Tsakos, and stayed at a luxury Paris hotel on a trip with him, with Tsakos footing the bill, the Journal reported.

The State Department's inspector general is investigating whether Guilfoyle received improper gifts, according to US media reports.

The revelations emerged as Rubio visited Europe last week, including a stop in Athens, where he declined to comment on the allegations.

title: The Australian housing challenge not being solved
text:
In brief Millions of spare bedrooms sit empty as downsizing stalls.

The costs of moving may be reshaping Australia's housing crunch.

Australia's rapidly growing older population has more wealth than ever and millions of spare bedrooms, yet financial incentives are pulling many away from downsizing, new research suggests.

Almost nine in ten older households (aged over 55) have at least one spare bedroom, and 60 per cent have two or more, twice the rate of households aged 25 to 54, new research published in the GemLife Downsizing Australia Report found.

The most popular homes among the 2,100 buyers over 50 looking to downsize surveyed were two and three-bedroom properties, offering low-maintenance living, good security, and proximity to amenities. But separate research indicates there is not enough of this housing being built.

There are about 13 million empty bedrooms across the country, but older people rely on spare rooms for grandchildren, visiting family, home offices or hobby rooms, Australian Housing and Urban Research Institute (AHURI) Managing Director Tom Alves told SBS News.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

He said their research has found 60 per cent of homeowners aged between 65 and 74 in 2001 were living in the same property 15 years later. And among those aged over 75, fewer than 15 per cent downsized.

AHURI has called for developer incentives to build medium-density housing designed for ageing.

People over 55 are projected to surge from the smallest group until 2028 to the largest in 2069. Credit: Australian Bureau of Statistics

Independent Kooyong MP Monique Ryan told SBS News that making better use of existing housing is one of the few short-term levers that can address the housing crisis.

"Downsizing can help younger families get into larger homes, unlock capital for older Australians, and limits urban sprawl," Ryan said.

Reasons to stay

The family home is a primary store of wealth for many older households, so releasing its equity can mean a loss of the age pension or other benefits, and more retirees are now carrying mortgage debt, Alves said.

"Other financial barriers to downsizing include upfront costs such as stamp duty incurred when purchasing a new home and agent fees incurred during the sales process," Alves said.

"Older households are also unlikely to be eligible for a traditional mortgage, which can create a blockage to moving."

Reasons to go

Changing the age pension assets test and building new senior housing within federally funded developments would help, Ryan said.

"Most important though is that the federal government should support the states in phasing in the replacement of stamp duty with a broad-based land tax, as has been suggested by the Productivity Commission and a number of other Treasury and Senate inquiries."

Stamp duty policy has shifted in South Australia, with exemptions for seniors purchasing some new homes, while concessions also exist in Victoria and the ACT.

A family home is generally exempt from the age pension assets test, but money unlocked through the sale of a house can become taxable if it is not used to purchase another principal home.

From January 2023, money from a home sale intended to buy a replacement can be exempt from an assets test for up to two years, with a conditional one-year extension. But any surplus profit can be taxed.

The federal government also lowered the age from 65 to 55 for downsizers to put up to $600,000 from their home sale into superannuation in January 2023.

The scheme was used by 15,800 people to contribute $4.165 billion in 2024–25, compared with 16,900 contributing $4.491 billion the previous year.

The wealth gap and transfer

As Australians retire with unprecedented levels of wealth, government spending on social safety nets for older Australians continues to grow.

Net tax and benefit changes for different age groups. Credit: Analysis by ANU Professor Robert Breunig

In 1971, just 17 per cent of Australians were over 55, while almost half the population was under 25. By 2028, these groups will be roughly even and by 2069 older people are projected to be the largest age group, and realestate.com.au senior economist Anne Flaherty says this is "going to be a big problem".

"Often the people who are you know living paycheck to paycheck are the ones who actually don't have access to a lot of the concessions that older Australians who who may be more cashed up have access to."

More reasons to stay

Another challenge is that the kinds of properties with the most capital growth are often larger houses, with more land in well-established suburbs, Flaherty said.

"So that's another incentive that people have not to leave their home, but to stay in that property and increase the capital gains they're going to see. (And) adult children can inherit that property, so it might be a way of keeping wealth in the family, which is inefficient because that home could have been used by someone who did need extra space."

Swapping stamp duty to a universal land tax is a "win-win for everyone over the long term", Flaherty said.

"The challenge, of course, is weaning state governments off stamp duty revenue over the short term is very difficult.

"This year is a good example of the problems with stamp duty, given the reduction in overall properties that have been selling. We're going to see a lot of state governments see their revenues take a big hit."

AHURI modelled the potential impact on house prices and rents of replacing stamp duty with a broad-based land tax, finding more affordable housing for both owner-occupiers and renters.

title: Australia's ruling on coal 'a clear signal' to the world, Pacific minister says
text:
In brief Tuvalu says a poorly attended climate summit still made an impact.

A landmark Australian ruling is being hailed beyond our shores.

Tuvalu's Climate Minister has hit back at claims that last week's Pre-COP event hosted by his country was a flop, while saying a phase-out of fossil fuels must be part of the discussion around COP31 in Türkiye.

Dr Maina Vakafua Talia also told SBS News his nation welcomed a landmark Australian High Court decision on coal and gas emissions, which provoked outcry from the mining sector, as a "clear signal" of moral responsibility.

Tuvalu, whose population numbers around 10,000, hosted a leader's gathering at last week's Pre-COP event shared with Fiji, part of a compromise struck by Australia to divide hosting rights with Türkiye.

The event came under heavy Australian media scrutiny, with shadow energy minister Dan Tehan labelling the event an "embarrassment" and a "flop" over the low number of leaders attending beyond a group from the Pacific.

While Talia acknowledged the Tuvalu meeting was only able to attract two global leaders from outside the Pacific (Timor-Leste and Mauritius), down from five initially expected, he described the turnout as "a big achievement for Tuvalu and for the Pacific."

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"We need to be very ambitious," he told SBS News in Canberra, talking up the event's shift from "a boring dialogue" to "a more moving, emotional engagement" focused on the challenges facing low-lying communities like his.

"The leaders were able to see for themselves, engage with the young ones, engage with our elders. One of the high representatives that came to Tuvalu told me, 'My heart bleeds when I saw the kids, when I saw our elders. Now I understand'."

The Taku Pakasoa Declaration agreed to at Pre-COP urged nations to act to keep the 1.5-degree climate target in reach, as well as increasing access to Climate Finance.

But there appears to be a diminishing appetite among nations for November's Antalya agreement to contain language focused on the phase-out of fossil fuels like Coal and Gas.

Türkiye's climate minister Murat Kurum, who will oversee the COP31 presidency, told the Guardian last week the world is "already in a transition" away from fossil fuels, reportedly suggesting the issue could be addressed indirectly through other means.

READ MORE The two-metre question that could wipe out a population

"If we are to discuss the 1.5 degrees, we are literally discussing the phasing out of fossil fuels," Talia said.

"We are talking about the backbone of some economies, but this is the reality that we have to face, and we really need to change the whole narrative, to change our priorities … to ensure that the survival of other peoples is always there."

Talia, who is set to share a related panel with energy minister Chris Bowen in Canberra, said he had faith Australia "can do more with the power that they have" to make the case for strong action, standing up to nations like India, Russia and China who are likely to argue for a moderate approach.

Climate ruling proof a moral responsibility

While leaders were gathering for Pre-COP, Australia's High Court delivered a landmark climate decision, finding in the case of Mount Pleasant Coal Mine in New South Wales, planning authorities must consider the entire carbon footprint of the project, including the emissions produced by the burning of fossil fuels overseas.

The decision referenced the 2025 International Court of Justice ruling brought on by Vanuatu, which found nations have international law obligations to protect the climate.

Talia said the Australian High Court ruling showed the impact of that ICJ precedent, and was one long-awaited by the Pacific nation.

"This is a good signal, a very clear signal, not just for the Pacific countries. It's really a moral responsibility for countries," he said.

The Australia-Tuvalu Falepili Union signed in 2024 was the first bilateral agreement to contain a significant pathway around climate mobility, with more than half the nation's population applying in the initial ballot.

"There is no treaty in this world we can allude to say that this is 100 per cent," Talia said, conceding "there are challenges, but they are manageable at the moment.

He said the risk of a brain drain was one his government would have to manage but rejected the claim the treaty was "creating an avenue for people to escape".

title: Is Australia prepared to cope with its 'modern-day success story'?
text:
IN BRIEF: Emergency departments will increasingly struggle to cope with an influx of elderly patients, a new report has found.

Experts say that older people are falling through the cracks at every level of the health and aged care systems.

Australians are living longer and the healthcare system is increasingly unable to cope, according to a new national report on the state of emergency departments (EDs).

The Australasian College of Emergency Medicine's (ACEM) third annual report notes that while Australia's ageing population is a "modern-day success story", the nation is not sufficiently prepared for the influx of elderly people into EDs.

From 2019 to 2024, the number of older people attending EDs increased by 16 per cent, compared with a 4 per cent increase among younger people, with half of all elderly presentations to an ED resulting in a hospital admission.

The group also found disparities in hospital care requirements between groups of older people.

While all non-Indigenous people aged 65 years and over were significantly more likely than younger people to be classified in higher urgency categories, arrive by ambulance and be admitted into hospital, that also holds for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people aged 50 years and over.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

ACEM president Dr Peter Allely said EDs were "far from ideal" environments to treat elderly patients, due to their "harsh lighting, loud noises and constant interruptions".

"We see too many frail people made afraid, confused and unwell by an unfamiliar environment, far away from their loved ones, familiar faces, supports and home comforts."

He said that, despite the "scale and predictability of demographic trends", governments across Australia had done little to prepare for the "volume and complexity of care needs" for the ageing population.

As a result, significant pressure was now being felt at "all levels" of the health system, including hospitals, primary and aged care facilities, and in-home support programs, he added.

ACEM is the organisation responsible for training emergency medicine specialists and setting standards for emergency care in Australia and New Zealand.

Across-the-board lack of preparedness

University of New South Wales professor in ageing health Lee-Fay Low agreed, saying she didn't think Australia had been doing anything long-term to prepare the health system for Australia's ageing population.

Similarly to Allely, Low said this lack of preparedness wasn't unique to hospitals, but could also be seen in primary care clinics, aged care facilities, and even among families.

Low, who is also leader of the Ageing and Health Research Group at the University of Sydney, said the ongoing aged care crisis was affecting people's ability to receive preventative care.

"Right now, because you have to wait for aged care, those things that might help might prevent you from going to emergency, like poor nutrition, ending up with an infection because your hygiene's not looked after."

READ MORE Aged care giant refunds $200,000 to residents over disputed living fees

Even since the Royal Commission into Aged Care handed down its final report in 2021, lengthy waitlists for aged care providers have seen many people go without crucial care, Low said.

"After the Aged Care Royal Commission, the government released more home care packages, allowing people to age in place without going into nursing homes. But that waitlist is a year long again now.

"The problem is that with the aged care reforms, things are worse now ... I mean, waiting a year is ridiculous.

"People living in their homes aren't really getting that aged care in a timely way, and that precedes these emergency visits."

READ MORE What 720 Australians reveal about ageing well — and the key to longevity

New health department data released yesterday found an average of 17 older Australians died while waiting to receive support at home care each day last year — an increase of more than a third on the previous year.

As of June 30, more than 106,000 Australians were on the official waiting list for a place in the Commonwealth-funded Support at Home program, while the ABC's Four Corners reported in August that the true number of people waiting was almost 154,000.

'Urgent action' needed

Older Australians made up only 17 per cent of the population in 2024 but accounted for almost a quarter of all ED presentations.

The ACEM report said that, without "urgent action", increased ED presentations by older people would disproportionately impact the healthcare system.

Using population growth modelling from the Australian Bureau of Statistics, the report projected a 177 per cent increase in total ED presentations between 2010 and 2050, noting projected increases of 242 per cent for people aged 65 to 84, and 411 per cent for people aged 85 and over.

ACEM is calling for federal, state and territory governments to urgently improve the quality of care older people receive across the health system, reduce ED demand, lift hospital capacity and provide sustainable hospital care for all Australians.

The government's latest Intergenerational Report projected rapid population ageing and falling fertility rates would fundamentally reshape the economy and budget out to 2065–66. By 2030, nearly one in five Australians will be aged 65 and over.

"The ratio of working people to older people is going to change substantively," Low said.

Allely warned that "Australia's health system and its health workforce are just not equipped for this demographic change."

More funding not the only remedy

Low said preparing for an ageing future required more than a funding boost.

"We always say we should have more funding, but I think where the funding is focused is important."

She also said proper reform would also require "an adjustment in presumptions and expectations Australians have for care as they get older".

"I think the presumption and the expectation in Australia is that when you get older, if you need care, you've paid taxes your whole life and the government will look after you. And that's already untrue, right? Aged care doesn't look after you straight away."

Low said a "national conversation" was needed to identify where the responsibility for care lies — whether it is with the government, or a co-contribution arrangement through which "as part of saving for retirement and super, that we also put aside some money, if we need help and we can pay for care".

Reforms also need to ensure the aged-care sector has a sufficient workforce, one-third of which is currently made up of migrants. Australia needs to reconsider decisions made around cutting migration, Low said.

She also suggested more families needed to start conversations about the "expectation that maybe mum and dad will need some help, and at that stage we might have to work less or chip in somehow to support the care".

But beyond families, she said, "this is not a conversation that we've had nationally".

There are two very distinct narratives emerging about artificial intelligence right now, and they’re both getting more extreme. You don’t need to be tuned into the debate to notice these two letters are appearing everywhere. AI is mentioned daily in the news, it’s brought up in work meetings, it appears in government policies and there’s barely a work conference where the topic if not discussed on and off stage. At one extreme are AI alarmists, who warn the technology is on a path to destruction. Marija Ercegovac What you think about the topic depends on which of the two extreme narratives you’re more likely to believe. At one end of the scale is the positive vision where the broad adoption of AI and robotics is on its way to creating a revolutionary new world. In this telling, goods and services will be dramatically cheaper, everyone will have access to high-quality healthcare and there will be little need to slave over much of the boring and time-consuming tasks that make up many people’s experience of work.

Advertisement

We do have one thing on our side right now, but not for much longer – and that is time. Elon Musk calls this “the age of abundance”, and Jeff Bezos predicted last week that a likely outcome of wide AI adoption would be the average person working just three days a week. Nvidia’s Jensen Huang told The New York Times last month that he thought it was a fallacy that AI would destroy jobs, and it will instead create even more jobs. Related Article Opinion

Holidays Why it’s time for you to ditch taking long annual holidays Tim Duggan Work columnist These grand visions of the future are driven primarily by the same tech oligarchs who are creating and selling this tech utopia. They want us to believe that everything will be better in their fantasies, with only pesky rights like privacy, truth and copyright needing to be sacrificed on the way there. At the other extreme end are AI alarmists, who conduct media tours warning us that the technology is on a path to destruction. It is self-improving at a pace that will soon be too powerful to control, they say, which could plausibly lead to cyberattacks, disinformation at scale, autonomous weapons or bioengineered pathogens that will threaten our very existence.

Advertisement

Many of these warnings on AI safety come from whistleblowing employees who have spent years working on the technology inside frontier labs, before deciding that they’ve now gone too far. One former Anthropic scientist, Evan Hubinger, resigned last month after giving a personal estimate that the risk of AI leading to the destruction of all humanity over the next decade is around 10 per cent. Related Article Opinion

Ask an expert From glowing feedback to undermining: Why has my boss turned on me? Jonathan Rivett Careers contributor These two extreme AI narratives – abundance or extinction – are both difficult to fully comprehend. Depending on which of them you lean towards will determine if you get excited every time an AI lab debuts a more powerful version of the technology, or if you wish they just downed their tools and stopped. But without any meaningful signs of regulation at their sources of these codes, primarily in the US and China, we’re all uncomfortably at their mercy. We do have one thing on our side right now, but not for much longer – and that is time. Despite all the recent advances, we are still at the stage of the technology when we can impact its outcome. It is still not too late for inbuilt safety checks across the leading frontier labs, government regulation, or even an agreed pause on the development to allow everyone to catch up. We need time to think about all the possible outcomes, formulate and debate legislation, agree on compromises and decide what kind of future we want.

Advertisement

That window of time is closing fast, but it’s still open for now. Is AI going to save us or destroy us? The answer depends on which of the two extreme ends of the narrative you’re more likely to believe, but the vast and growing valley between them is too wide to ignore. text:

Breaking NationalVictoriaVictorian election ‘Oh no’: $285m COVID cover-up exposed by whistleblowers Patrick Hatch Updated October 15, 2026 — 2:39pm ,first published 11:27am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items.
