Two senior bureaucrats tried to cover up a suspected $285 million bungle that saw COVID-19 payments made to ineligible businesses by withholding information from their boss and government ministers. A report by the Independent Broad-based Anti-corruption Commission (IBAC) released on Thursday revealed that “false and misleading information” was provided to then-minister Martin Pakula in November 2021 in a bid to hide the fact that almost one quarter of the state’s program grants had been paid in error. Bourke Street was virtually empty during a Melbourne lockdown in 2020. Jason South The corruption watchdog’s investigation focused on the $4.5 billion Business Costs Assistance Program, which delivered up to $97,200 to businesses affected by state’s pandemic lockdown measures in 2020 and 2021. IBAC found that in November 2021, public servants in the Department of Jobs, Precincts and Regions identified that more than 9000 ineligible businesses had claimed an estimated $285 million worth of grants by backdating their GST registrations.

Advertisement

GST registration was a key criterion for eligibility, but the department did not appreciate the risk that businesses could legally backdate this by up to four years. Related Article Analysis

IBAC Victoria’s anti-corruption watchdog finally has teeth. These are its new powers At the time of assessing businesses, the department checked eligibility using a live database that updated as people backdated their GST registrations, rather than a static dataset that would have reflected eligibility at the time each grant was announced, IBAC found. Though the department initially estimated the total amount to be $285 million, the commission’s own analysis found that approximately $257 million was paid to ineligible businesses, with $108 million going to businesses that reported no activity in the six months leading up to the pandemic. To date, recipients who incorrectly received the grants have repaid about $8 million to the state government. Another $5 million is being returned through repayment plans, IBAC said.

Advertisement

The report says the department’s acting director of COVID-19 grants policy exclaimed “oh no” upon realising that almost one-fifth of the program’s funds had gone to ineligible applicants, and later remarked that it was “astonishing to realise how many snuck through”. In November 2021, a figure for “backdated GST registration … paid in error” losses was included in a draft Standing Directions report intended for the department’s secretary, Simon Phemister, and Pakula, then the minister for industry support and recovery. The investigation probed corrupt conduct by senior officials in the Department of Jobs, Precincts and Regions. The initial figure was listed as $8.92 million, but was revised to $251.9 million following further analysis by the department’s Integrity Services Unit. However, on November 30, 2021, the item was deleted from the report entirely at the request of a deputy secretary, the report says.

Advertisement

The deputy secretary told IBAC that the deletion followed “discussion and a decision that was reached above me”, noting that the department’s associate secretary was the most immediate person involved in those discussions. Editor's pick Opinion

Victorian election Forget political dust-ups – some of parliament’s best work never makes the front page Chip Le Grand State political editor The associate secretary told IBAC they did not draft or amend the report, or tell anyone to amend it. At the time, they believed the analysis leading to the overpayment figure was flawed, they said. A text message provided to IBAC showed the associate secretary telling the deputy secretary on December 3, 2025, that “I don’t think that problem re GST backdating overpayments is a problem. Phew”. However, IBAC said the associate secretary should have reported the analysis to the secretary, even if he disagreed with it.

Advertisement

IBAC said that “misleading information was subsequently created and disseminated over an extended period of time” as part of the cover-up, including to now-premier Ben Carroll in 2022 after he replaced Pakula as the relevant minister. The associate secretary also withheld key information from the Victorian Ombudsman, IBAC found. IBAC Commissioner Victoria Elliott said the investigation, named Operation Harmonia, uncovered behaviour contrary to the Victorian Public Sector code of conduct and “a clear failure to act in line with the high integrity standards expected of Victoria’s public officers”. Former minister for jobs, Martin Pakula, at a COVID-related press conference in 2021. Robert Cianflone/Getty Images “While officers within the department spoke up, their leaders failed to act, meaning the government was left uninformed and unable to move quickly to address this suspected significant loss of public funds,” he said.

Advertisement

Elliott applauded whistleblowers from within the Victorian public service who alerted IBAC to the cover-up and triggered its investigation. “Your bravery is critical in ensuring this conduct is not only exposed but that Victoria’s public sector can take these findings and apply the learnings to their own organisations,” he said. IBAC said it believed Phemister, the secretary, was not informed about the suspected loss, and that he was therefore unable to inform the minister about it. Pakula also told IBAC he was never informed of the issue. The report does not name the deputy secretary or associate secretary involved. title: Lung cancer rates in non-smokers like Pope Leo are rising. How can you catch it early?
text:

LifestyleHealth & wellnessLung cancer Lung cancer rates in non-smokers like Pope Leo are rising. How can you catch it early? Lauren Ironmonger Updated October 15, 2026 — 2:08pm ,first published 11:06am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Pope Leo XIV has announced he underwent surgery for lung cancer, after doctors detected a small growth on his lung during a routine health check. The Vatican said the Pope had lung adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer. Leo, 71, is a non-smoker. In Australia, lung cancer is the leading cause of death from cancer, killing more men and women annually than breast and prostate cancer combined, and is the fifth most diagnosed cancer. Despite this, detection rates remain low. Why? And what can you do to catch it early? Pope Leo is recovering from surgery for lung cancer. AP Photo/Andrew Medichini

Advertisement

What causes lung cancer? Globally, cases of lung cancer are increasing, particularly among young women who never smoked, according to research published by The World Health Organisation last year. The link between smoking and lung cancer is well-established, with co-ordinated public health campaigns over the past few decades helping rates of smoking drop significantly. This year, Australian researchers published a review with the strongest evidence yet that vaping is likely to cause lung and oral cancer. But Fraser Brims, deputy director of the Institute for Respiratory Health and professor at Curtin University, says environmental factors – like air pollution and radon, a natural gas – occupational exposure to dust, asbestos and silica, and genetics and family history can all contribute.

Advertisement

“One of the really important messages is that anybody with lungs can get lung cancer, and it’s certainly not just about smoking,” he says. Editor's pick Science The ‘unworthy’ cancer with a terrible survival rate and the program seeking to change it Evidence that exposure to incense or candle smoke causes cancer – despite information commonly circulated online – is inconclusive and there is no known risk, says Brims. Nor is risk merely shaped by individual lifestyle choices. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples disproportionately bear the burden of the disease in terms of diagnosis and mortality, alongside those living in regional and rural areas and from lower socioeconomic backgrounds.

Advertisement

Mark Brooke, Lung Foundation chief executive, says while most lung cancers have no symptoms in the early stages, the four most common signs are coughing up blood, persistent coughing, fatigue and weight loss. Lung cancer screening is Australia’s only risk-based screening program, unlike the bowel and breast cancer programs, which are age-based. Monique Westermann The stigma Despite plummeting smoking rates in countries like Australia, and rising lung cancer among non-smokers, the disease still carries stigma. “Australia is one of the worst in terms of this assumption and judging people against that. In no other type of cancer do we judge by a risk factor,” says Brims.

Advertisement

In Australia, 28 per cent of people admit they have less sympathy for someone with lung cancer compared with other forms of cancer, while one-third are unable to name one symptom. Lingering stigma, Brooke says, influences investment and donations. Compared to breast cancer, which has higher survivorship rates, lung cancer research receives around 30 per cent less funding. Loading How can you catch lung cancer early? Oncologists said Leo’s prognosis was “excellent” even before the operation due to early detection, according to the Associated Press.

Advertisement

Advertisement

Brooke says there is no evidence for making it a population-based screening program. “We have to weigh up the economic benefit versus the risks of having our population exposed to a CT scan on a frequent basis,” he says, adding non-specific screening also risks returning false positives, exposing individuals to invasive and potentially harmful medical interventions. Lung nodules – small growths found in lung tissue – can be found in up to half of people screened, but most are not related to cancer, says Brims. “It’s for us and medical teams to work out which ones we need to be most concerned about … the screening program’s process has so far proven very effective,” he says, adding they are working to identify and effectively target population groups most at risk. The Lung Foundation is calling on the government to increase eligibility to individuals aged 50 to 75 with a direct family history and those at risk of occupational exposure, alongside greater government research funding and more support for those diagnosed and their carers.

Advertisement

If you are concerned about your lung cancer risk or exhibit any “red flag” symptoms, like a lingering cough, Brooke urges individuals to “talk to your GP, explore your options for a CT scan and don’t delay”. Zenith Minerals’ bid to connect the dots between two gold deposits at its Consolidated Dulcie project in Western Australia is gaining some serious momentum, with the drill bit jagging a solid six-metre hit grading 4.14 grams per tonne (g/t) gold. The intercept included a higher-grade three-metre core going an eye-catching 7.75g/t gold. Impressively, the company says all 14 holes assayed at its Dulcie Central target have now intersected gold mineralisation, bolstering its interpretation of a continuous gold system. Zenith Minerals’ drilling at its Consolidated Dulcie Gold Project in Western Australia. The results come from a recently completed 34-hole reverse circulation drilling campaign across the broader project, with assays for 15 more holes now in hand. Zenith’s program is designed to test the roughly 600m strike gap between its existing Dulcie North and more southerly Dulcie deposits. Other results from the Dulcie Central corridor include a shallow, 10-metre intercept at 0.84g/t gold from just 48m, with another hole producing a three-metre strike running 1.59g/t gold from a similar depth. A third hole returned 2m at 1.57g/t gold from 97m and 3m grading 1.14g/t gold from 134m, hinting at the prospect of gold continuity at depth.

‘Every Dulcie Central hole assayed so far has intersected gold across the approximately 600-metre gap.’ Zenith Minerals managing director Andrew Smith Notably, drilling at Zenith’s nearby Scott’s Grey prospect, one kilometre south of Dulcie Central also assayed solid numbers, with one hole hitting 4m at 3.05g/t gold from 71m, including a richer one-metre section at a hefty 7.17g/t. Further south again, at Dulcie South, a one-metre intercept came in at 3.86g/t gold from 128m. The Consolidated Dulcie project already hosts a significant JORC-compliant inferred mineral resource of 21.3 million tonnes grading 1g/t gold for 675,000 ounces across a 6-kilometre mineralised corridor. The grounds sit within the revered Southern Cross–Forrestania gold belt and benefit from granted mining leases and proximity to regional processing infrastructure at Marvel Loch and Edna May, placing it in prime real estate. Zenith Minerals managing director Andrew Smith said: “Every Dulcie Central hole assayed so far has intersected gold, with one hole returning the strongest intersection of the programme to date. These results continue to support the interpretation that gold mineralisation extends across the approximately 600-metre gap between Dulcie North and Dulcie.” While the company’s current program is focused on growing the resource, historical hits at the broader project have delivered some stunners such as 32m at 9.4g/t gold and 3m at an eye-watering 70g/t gold, highlighting the system’s high-grade pedigree.

Elsewhere, Zenith has a foothold on the promising Red Mountain gold project in Queensland, where previous drilling included a whopping 139.7m at 1.05g/t gold from 225m, which featured a richer 2-metre core assaying 21.03g/t gold within a broader 14.2m section grading 4.62g/t gold. Drilling has since traced gold mineralisation beyond 700m vertical depth, reinforcing the continuity of a broad intrusion-related gold system. The company also holds a 25 per cent free-carried interest at the emerging Earaheedy zinc project north-east of Wiluna in WA, alongside an indirect 26 per cent stake in the historic Cowarra gold project south of Canberra in New South Wales. Rounding out the portfolio, its Split Rocks lithium project in WA showcases an inferred JORC resource of 11.9Mt grading 0.72 per cent lithium oxide. With assays for 24 of the 34 holes back from the lab, attention is likely to turn to the final 10 holes, also all drilled within the promising 600-metre Dulcie Central corridor. The company expects a batch of results in late October, completing the final piece of the puzzle needed to assess a potential maiden mineral resource for the target area. A positive outcome could see Zenith stitch together the Dulcie North and Dulcie deposits into one much bigger, continuous orebody. With a 100 per cent hit rate so far in the critical gap zone and a history of high-grade hits in the area, the market will likely be keenly awaiting that final newsflow, which could potentially set the stage for Zenith to clock a significant resource upgrade at the already well-endowed project. title: Iron Bear retakes full control of generational Canadian iron ore giant
text:

In the junior mining sector, securing a cashed-up global giant as a partner is often seen as a final validation, the golden ticket. So, when an iron ore major such as Brazil’s Vale walks away from a farm-in deal, the market’s first instinct is often to head for the exits. But every now and then, a closer look at the details reveals a different story - one where the junior partner is perhaps left holding the keys to a kingdom. This looks to be the intriguing situation unfolding for ASX-listed Iron Bear Resources at its namesake project in the Labrador Trough, the heartland of Canada’s premier emerging iron ore sector. Iron Bear’s namesake project sits in Labrador, Canada, one of the country’s premier iron ore districts. After a period of collaboration that saw its partner Vale sink US$18 million (A$25.8 million) into de-risking the colossal project in eastern Canada, the Brazilian behemoth has signalled its intent to bow out. Its departure leaves Iron Bear holding 100 per cent of a project with a recently completed prefeasibility study (PFS) valuing it at a staggering US$9 billion (A$12.8B) in net present value (NPV) - and that’s just on its conservative scenario. Yet the market has not exactly rewarded Iron Bear for its newfound freedom. Since Vale’s decision, Iron Bear’s valuation has been cut almost in half, suggesting investors have viewed the loss of the major partner as a doomsday event for future financing.

Advertisement

However, the market’s reaction appears to have overshadowed the enormous scale of Iron Bear’s multi-generational resource, its premium iron ore pellet product and the strategic importance of North American iron ore supply for cleaner steel production. For Vale, the decision, while surprising given the project’s immense value, fits with its broader shift towards investment opportunities closer to home. The iron ore giant has increasingly turned its attention to expanding its South American copper operations - pulling from the BHP playbook - and future local rare earth initiatives. Simultaneously, the company remains hamstrung by an enormous financial liability stemming from its 2010s tailings dam disasters. With billions tied up in remediation, compensation and dam decommissioning back home, a US$5 billion (A$7.15 billion) development some 9000 kilometres away has become a difficult proposition for an increasingly Brazilian-owned organisation, with lofty expectations of domestic reinvestment. Vale’s growing appetite for copper and its renewed focus on South American investments may have inadvertently dealt Iron Bear a winning hand. With full ownership restored, the junior is now free to pursue offtake agreements, streaming deals, financing or strategic partnership opportunities, all on its own terms. In mining, you rarely get someone else to do the heavy lifting before handing you back the whole prize. By any measure, the Iron Bear project is a monster. It hosts a JORC resource of 13.6 billion tonnes grading 30 per cent iron and containing more of the steelmaking metal than Rio Tinto’s fabled “Pilbara Killer” Simandou, in Guinea, West Africa. The resource at Iron Bear is so vast that its initial 44-year mine plan touches less than a quarter of the known deposit.

Advertisement

The company says the deposit is a typical Labrador Trough taconite, a hard, iron-rich rock deposit that has underpinned mining in the region for over half a century. The district already hosts successful producers, including ASX-listed Champion Iron, whose Bloom Lake operation is a proven economic model for turning this type of ore into high-value products. However, Iron Bear would seem to be playing in a different league. Its maiden probable ore reserve of 3.3 billion tonnes is roughly five times bigger than Bloom Lake’s entire reserve base and its total resource is an order of magnitude greater. It was this sheer, multi-generational scale that attracted Vale to Canada, leading to a binding agreement that would have seen the major fund up to US$138 million in development costs to earn a whopping 75 per cent stake. For a junior developer, the deal was transformative. It wasn’t just the funding; it was the third-party validation and access to Vale’s immense technical expertise. Over the subsequent period, Vale’s top engineers worked alongside the Iron Bear crew, deploying serious capital to advance the project towards a PFS. That study, delivered by the highly respected Hatch engineering group, landed with a thud, confirming the project’s world-class potential. The PFS outlined a 44-year operation at 23 million tonnes of iron ore annually. It projected a post-tax NPV of US$9 billion and an internal rate of return of 15.2 per cent - more than suitable for major players looking for multi-decade production.

Advertisement

Perhaps even more importantly, the whole operation is slated to run entirely on extremely cheap, renewable hydropower. And with the Canadian government actively encouraging new resource development while keeping emissions low for its citizens, a high-purity critical minerals project like Iron Bear could be just the ticket. Recent federal legislation has reopened accelerated project approvals for “projects of national significance” - a status that Iron Bear has already applied for. If successful, this could significantly shorten the permitting timeline in Labrador and further de-risk the project for investment. Adding to the robust economics is the project’s prime location for infrastructure. It sits less than 35 kilometres from an open-access, heavy-haul railway that connects directly to the deep-water port of Sept-Iles, North America’s biggest mineral port. Iron Bear’s premium Direct Reduction pellets, crucial feed for DR steel production, a clean technology to produce steel using natural gas or hydrogen instead of coal. Equally compelling, the study confirmed the project’s ability to produce a premium product tailor-made for the future of steelmaking.

Advertisement

Iron Bear’s pilot plant testwork has confirmed the taconite ore can be upgraded to a 71 per cent iron concentrate suitable for the increasingly sought after Direct Reduction (DR) steelmaking. The pathway to so-called “green steel” is achievable only through DR plants that can be powered by natural gas or, ultimately, green hydrogen, slashing carbon emissions compared to traditional coal-fired blast furnaces. The premium DR grade product commands a hefty premium over benchmark 62 per cent iron ore fines, with Iron Bear tipping demand to surge 50 per cent over the next decade as steelmakers chase cleaner production. With premium DR-grade pellets fetching up to US$225 a tonne in the spot market, the right offtake deal could lock in future sales while delivering valuable upfront financing to help bankroll the mine’s development. Armed with A$15.3 million in cash, a completed PFS and full ownership of its colossal Canadian asset, Iron Bear now resembles a newly single eligible bachelor - suddenly free to court top-tier offtakers on its own terms. Losing a major partner is rarely cause for celebration, yet Iron Bear has emerged with a project scrutinised and de-risked alongside one of the world’s biggest iron ore producers, with the entire prize back in its own hands. The company’s challenge now is to turn a significant head start into a development deal worthy of a once-in-a-generation resource and its US$9 billion NPV, potentially cementing its place among North America’s most strategic iron ore assets. Nick Blakey is an excellent footballer, an All-Australian defender in the prime of his career with speed and a lethal left foot. North Melbourne officials were excited to land him in this trade period for that reason, but it was no ordinary trade that sent him from Sydney to the Kangaroos. Nick Blakey dons the North Melbourne guernsey. Nathan John, North Melbourne FC That’s because Blakey remains one of four AFL players still subject to a Victoria Police investigation into allegations of sexual assault at the Pullman hotel, where the Swans were staying after beating Essendon at the MCG in round 23. The five players who were suspended by Sydney for breaching behavioural standards, including Blakey, have consistently denied any wrongdoing. None have been charged.

Advertisement

But it remains a challenging situation, particularly for the women who made the allegations. Because, less than two months later and with that police investigation unresolved, a club board decided to offer one of the players involved a spot in their team, and for a salary close to $12 million over eight years. In what world does that happen? We have the answer: in the AFL, where a club exists to win and any concerns about behaviour can be addressed with an apology and a promise to do better.

Advertisement

Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 From Pullman to pulling power: How Nick Blakey profited from scandal and the AFL’s strange economy That is all Blakey can really do. His dissatisfaction with the Swans shows he doesn’t believe his involvement in whatever may have happened at the Pullman has been fairly reflected in Sydney’s decisions. My discomfort with the trade is not directed towards him. My issue is that the club’s decision and the AFL’s willingness to wave it through makes all the virtue-signalling words the industry uses ring hollow. The league creates an impression that it is a leader on social issues, which carries an assumed yet laughable mortgage on defining what makes someone “a good person”. CEO Andrew Dillon wrote in the days after the Pullman incident: “Our first question should not be what this means for a football club. It should be whether our actions match the standards we stand for and the community expects of us. “As a sport, and as an industry, we are clear about the standards we expect and the values we stand for and the need to uphold them.

Advertisement

“Being clear about our standards also means being prepared to act when those standards are not met.” Sydney acted. They took a strong stand to show they stood for more than just winning, and it cost them. AFL chief executive Andrew Dillon made a strong statement about the standards players and officials should meet in the days following the Pullman incident. Eddie Jim North Melbourne certainly acted. They now have Blakey on more money than anyone else at the club. The Roos showed it was one club taking a stand, rather than the industry, by seizing on the opportunity Sydney’s approach presented them.

Advertisement

Related Article AFL 2026 Wife of top AFL executive voices concern over Nick Blakey trade deal The AFL will say it can’t dictate to the clubs what they do during trade period, particularly during an active police investigation. But every decision reflects on the league, and the size of the deal is incongruous with those words from a month ago. The AFL waving the trade through implies, whether true or not, that the league knows something we don’t. Surely a club wouldn’t sign a player to such a long-term deal and give away such draft capital if it wasn’t confident he would line up the next season. Actions speak louder than words and the trade showed in stark reality that the defining feature of the game at the highest level is how well you play it and the rest can be, to use a football cliche, worked through. That’s fine and not unexpected, but spare us the bullshit. The right many in the game assume – to lead on social issues – is disappearing before our eyes. That’s unfortunate because their power to influence is unquestionable.

Advertisement

That’s why this trade is challenging for those who love footy, as the decisions the players made that night – regardless of whether anything criminal may have occurred – were out of step with the expectations that clubs and supporters have of players. Seeing one of them rewarded financially so soon after just felt wrong. North Melbourne’s offer is challenging for volunteers working their guts out to maintain great community football clubs with inclusive environments for no reward except in giving people a safe place to gather on the weekend. It will be challenging to people within the North Melbourne Football Club and at other AFL clubs who sell a vision that tries to create a purpose beyond merely winning. North Melbourne players and staff members are now representatives of the decision to bring Blakey on board – whether they like it or not.

Advertisement

They will be muted in what they can say because anyone who objects is in for a fight. The machine operates at full tilt to support those who entertain rather than complain. The Kangaroos decided to communicate the reasons behind their decision to staff and their premiership-winning AFLW team. The forum wasn’t an opportunity to approve or object to those reasons, as such. It was so that everyone understood the club’s reasoning, while giving a chance for questions about how to respond to stakeholders when queries about the decision inevitably arise. Loading But even if it had been a forum for debate, would anyone who objected have been perceived as difficult? The Roos have built a strong culture under impressive leadership from the president Sonja Hood and CEO Jen Watt. And they are a football club with the primary aim of winning games. That’s understood and has been reinforced time and time again across all the clubs.

Advertisement

Perhaps it’s the pretence that it means something more that irks the most. The salient question for North to answer is this: what gives them the confidence they can absorb Blakey into their program and maintain a strong culture when questions abound about the players’ behaviour at the Pullman? AFL players (from left) Chad Warner, James Jordon, Isaac Heeney and Nick Blakey are still subject to a police investigation. The Age Having entered into such a big contract, will they pull up behaviour if performance is strong? They can argue they showed that capacity when they cut Tarryn Thomas for “inappropriate treatment of women” in 2024.

Advertisement

Meanwhile, the league will argue it can’t do anything of substance until the police investigation concludes. Currently, it seems the outcome of that police investigation will determine the AFL and industry’s standards. Because the hand-wringing that followed the Pullman incident, and the concern for the women making the complaints that were so frequently expressed before footy issues were discussed back in August, are no longer part of the script. I am not in a position to lecture and won’t go down that path. But now that we understand through research, such as what’s laid out on Our Watch’s website, that “gender inequality sets the underlying context for violence against women”, we should all be prepared to do better.

title: Twin brothers win Lotto twice in two years
text:
Twin brothers have defied the odds and are planning to hit the road after they celebrated their second lotto win within two years.

The Albany brothers, 65, from Western Australia's Great Southern, shared a $1m Millionaire Medley prize within two years of winning Set For Life.

The first win helped them buy their sister's home, now they can pay off the property and hit the road.

Both winning tickets were purchased from Clark's Newsagency in Albany.

One of the lucky brothers said he bought the ticket after his dentist appointment was cancelled.

"When I got home, I realised I'd bought a Slikpik and forgotten to get my usual numbers as well," he said.

"I wouldn't usually ever buy more than one ticket a day, but when I realised I'd only bought the Slikpik, I thought I'd pop back because I like playing the same numbers.

"I know it's completely random, but it's what I like to do."

The second trip to the retailer resulted in a System 8 entry that secured the $1 million prize.

"We're set now," one brother said.

"We've worked physically demanding jobs our whole lives but now we can relax a bit more, pay the house off and then we both want to get caravans so we can travel around Australia together."

The twin brothers have won Lotto twice within two years.

While one brother is dreaming of life on the road, the other has already celebrated in his own way.

"I bought myself a watch because you have to treat yourself a bit," he said.

"I also like disco and dancing, so I might celebrate with my girlfriend."

Lotterywest spokesman Nikki Wilson-Smith said it was rare to welcome the same players back to the Winners Room for a second major prize.

"Winning a major prize is a memorable moment for any player, but to experience two significant wins within such a short period is remarkable," she said.

"It's wonderful to see these brothers using their prizes to secure their future and enjoy retirement together."
